Trump Strikes 'Lowest-Price' Drug Deals with 9 Mid-Sized Pharma Firms, Securing $19.6 Billion in US Investment
Add to Google Preferred Sources
The Trump administration has signed Most Favored Nation (MFN) drug pricing agreements with nine mid-sized pharmaceutical companies, including Alcon, Astellas, Teva, UCB, and Sun Pharma. In exchange for lowering US prescription drug prices to the lowest levels paid by other developed nations, these companies have committed to investing more than $19.6 billion in US manufacturing facilities and donating critical active pharmaceutical ingredients to the strategic national stockpile. The agreements bring the total number of pharmaceutical companies under MFN deals to 26, representing 89% of the US branded drug market. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates approximately $600 billion in cost savings over the next decade. Shares of the publicly traded companies involved showed little movement immediately following the announcement.
Key Elements
Donald Trump
White House
Teva Pharmaceutical
UCB
Sun Pharma
Astellas Pharma
Kyowa Kirin
CSL
MFN Drug Pricing Agreement
Medicaid
Alcon
BeOne Medicines
BridgeBio
The US government has partnered with nine global mid-sized pharmaceutical companies to lower prescription drug prices to the lowest levels paid by other developed nations, in exchange for securing $19.6 billion (approximately 26.8 trillion won) in US manufacturing investment from these firms. The Trump administration's strategy of pursuing both drug price reductions and supply chain reshoring is now extending to mid-sized pharmaceutical companies.
The White House announced on the 31st (local time) that it had signed new Most Favored Nation (MFN) drug pricing agreements with nine companies: Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceutical, and UCB. MFN is a policy that aligns US prescription drug prices with the lowest prices paid by other wealthy nations, and has been a cornerstone of the Trump administration's drug pricing policy since last year.
According to a report released on the 1st by the Korea Bio Association's Bio Economy Research Center, state Medicaid programs across the US will now receive MFN pricing on drugs produced by these nine companies. The targeted disease areas include hemophilia, Parkinson's disease, macular degeneration, glaucoma, liver disease, skin conditions, and various cancers—chronic and rare diseases with high treatment costs. The White House plans to apply the same MFN pricing to innovative new drugs these companies launch in the future, reducing the drug cost burden on American patients.
With this agreement, the total number of pharmaceutical companies under MFN deals with the Trump administration has grown to 26. The nine new companies join the existing 17 large pharmaceutical firms that previously reached agreements, including Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Amgen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Gilead, GSK, Merck, Novartis, Sanofi, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, and Regeneron. These companies now account for 89% of the US branded drug market. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates that the MFN policy will generate approximately $600 billion (about 820.9 trillion won) in cost savings over the next decade.
In exchange for lower drug prices, the pharmaceutical companies are committing substantial capital to strengthen US production and supply chains. The nine companies participating in this agreement have pledged to invest a total of more than $19.6 billion in US manufacturing facilities in the near term—approximately 26.8 trillion won.
Stockpiling of critical active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) in the US is also expanding. UCB plans to donate 163 tons of the anticonvulsant levetiracetam to the US Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Reserve (SAPIR). Sun Pharma will provide 71.4 tons of the antibiotic clindamycin and 6.75 tons of doxycycline, while Teva will supply 45 tons of metronidazole and 4.8 tons of the hypertension drug amlodipine. Astellas will also donate 25 kilograms of tacrolimus, used to prevent rejection in organ transplant patients, to the stockpile.
This signals that drug pricing policy is evolving beyond simply reducing patient medication costs and is now being combined with a US-centric pharmaceutical supply chain restructuring strategy. While global pharmaceutical companies have been expanding their US manufacturing facilities recently, the critical stages of API production remain concentrated overseas, particularly in China and India. This is the backdrop for the US government's move to manage not just finished drug production but also APIs as strategic assets.
Industry observers believe tariff considerations played a significant role in these companies' decisions to participate. The White House did not disclose specific incentives or tariff benefits offered to the pharmaceutical companies in this announcement, but trade tariffs have served as a key negotiating tool in previous MFN negotiations. In fact, announcements from some companies, including UCB, suggest that tariff exemptions were a major factor in the MFN negotiations.
Notably, unlike previous MFN agreements dominated by large American and European pharmaceutical companies, this round includes India's Sun Pharma, Israel's Teva, Japan's Astellas and Kyowa Kirin, and Australia's CSL. Observers say the Trump administration's pressure for drug price reductions and expanded US production is now spreading in earnest to global mid-sized pharmaceutical companies.
Shares of the publicly traded companies involved showed little movement immediately following the announcement. Teva closed down 1.1% in regular trading before rising 2% in after-hours trading. BeOne Medicines held at a decline of about 2%, while BridgeBio was nearly flat in regular trading before ticking up slightly after hours. Alcon also showed little change. Year-to-date, Teva is up 16% and BeOne Medicines up 18%, while Alcon is down 9% and BridgeBio remains near flat.
This agreement demonstrates that the Trump administration's drug pricing pressure campaign, which began in 2025, has evolved to a new level. President Trump signed an executive order in 2025 demanding MFN pricing and sent letters to 17 of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies warning of import tariffs if they failed to lower US drug prices. Pfizer was the first to reach an agreement in September 2025, followed by AstraZeneca and EMD Serono. In November of the same year, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk agreed to significantly cut prices on their popular obesity and diabetes treatments, and in December, nine major pharmaceutical companies—including Amgen, BMS, Gilead, GSK, Merck, Novartis, and Sanofi—signed on the same day. Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie joined in January of this year, with Regeneron becoming the latest to sign in April.

Pharmaceutical Defoamers Market Outlook to 2035
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global
Pharmaceutical Defoamers market
, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global pharmaceutical defoamers market is entering a phase of sustained expansion, underpinned by structural shifts in biopharmaceutical manufacturing. As drug developers intensify cell culture processes, adopt single-use bioreactors, and move toward continuous manufacturing, the demand for GMP-compliant foam control agents is rising across drug substance production. Industry estimates suggest the market will grow at a compound annual rate of 5–7% from 2026 to 2035, with bioprocessing applications accounting for roughly 60–70% of total volume.
Silicone-based defoamers currently dominate, representing about 55–65% of global volume, owing to their chemical inertness and broad regulatory acceptance. However, non-silicone alternatives such as polyether-based and fatty-acid ester formulations are gaining traction in cell and gene therapy workflows, where silicone can interfere with protein purification or cell viability.
Supply chain qualification remains the primary friction point: downstream buyers, including CDMOs and large pharma, depend on a limited number of approved suppliers that provide comprehensive documentation packages covering residual solvents, elemental impurities, sterilization validation, and change-notification protocols. This qualification barrier concentrates high-value procurement among five to seven globally active manufacturers. The market is also witnessing a shift toward pre-qualified, ready-to-use formulations and customized molecular-weight distributions, while regulatory scrutiny on extractables and leachables is intensifying.
Regional sourcing strategies are emerging, with buyers dual-sourcing from regional and Asian suppliers, and Indian manufacturers expanding FDA-inspected facilities to capture a growing share of export-oriented demand.
The baseline scenario for the pharmaceutical defoamers market points to steady growth through 2035, driven by the expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and the increasing complexity of drug modalities. The market is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 5.8% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 172 by 2035 relative to 2025. Bioprocessing remains the dominant application, fueled by the adoption of intensified cell culture processes, single-use bioreactors, and continuous manufacturing. These technologies increase volumetric consumption of defoamers per batch, as foam control becomes more critical in high-density cultures and prolonged operation.
Cell and gene therapy workflows are emerging as a high-growth segment, requiring low-toxicity defoamers that do not compromise cell viability or downstream purification. Regulatory requirements, including ICH Q3D and USP , are pushing suppliers to generate comprehensive extractables and leachables data, favoring incumbents with deep analytical capabilities. The qualification cycle for new defoamer sources remains long—typically 12–18 months—creating high switching costs and reinforcing the market positions of established suppliers.
Raw material input costs, particularly for silicone oils and polyols, are subject to volatility, but supply chain diversification and dual-sourcing strategies are mitigating risks. The competitive landscape is characterized by a few global players with strong regulatory expertise and a growing number of regional manufacturers, especially in Asia, who are expanding their FDA-inspected facilities. Overall, the market is expected to benefit from the continued growth of biologics, the rise of personalized medicine, and the increasing need for robust foam control in complex manufacturing processes.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
Expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity, particularly for monoclonal antibodies and recombinant proteins, increases the volumetric demand for foam control agents in fermentation and cell culture processes.
Adoption of single-use bioreactors and intensified cell culture processes raises the frequency and volume of defoamer dosing per batch, as foam formation becomes more pronounced in high-density cultures.
Growth of cell and gene therapy workflows requires low-toxicity defoamers that do not interfere with cell viability or downstream purification, creating demand for non-silicone and specialized formulations.
Regulatory requirements for GMP compliance and comprehensive documentation, including extractables and leachables data, favor established suppliers and drive demand for high-quality, validated defoamer products.
Shift toward continuous manufacturing in pharmaceutical production increases the need for reliable, consistent foam control over extended operation periods, boosting consumption of ready-to-use defoamer formulations.
Rising investment in bioprocessing R&D and the development of novel drug modalities, including mRNA and viral vectors, expands the application scope for defoamers in research and development settings.
Potential Growth Constraints
Long qualification cycles, typically 12–18 months, for new defoamer sources create high switching costs and limit the ability of new entrants to displace established suppliers.
Raw material input cost volatility, particularly for silicone oils and polyols, can pressure profit margins and lead to price fluctuations for end users.
Regulatory scrutiny on extractables and leachables, including ICH Q3D and USP , increases the cost and complexity of product development and registration, particularly for smaller suppliers.
Potential interference of silicone-based defoamers with protein purification or cell viability in certain sensitive workflows restricts their use in cell and gene therapy applications, requiring alternative formulations.
Supply chain disruptions, including geopolitical tensions and trade barriers, can affect the availability of raw materials and finished products, prompting buyers to maintain larger inventories.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
Bioprocessing and Drug Manufacturing (estimated share: 65%)
Bioprocessing and drug manufacturing represent the largest end-use segment for pharmaceutical defoamers, accounting for an estimated 65% of global demand. This segment includes fermentation and cell culture processes used to produce monoclonal antibodies, recombinant proteins, vaccines, and other biologics. The shift toward intensified processes, such as fed-batch and perfusion cultures, increases cell densities and metabolic activity, leading to greater foam formation. Consequently, the volumetric consumption of defoamers per batch rises.
Single-use bioreactors, which are increasingly adopted for their flexibility and reduced contamination risk, require pre-qualified defoamer formulations that are compatible with disposable bags and tubing. The demand for GMP-compliant defoamers with comprehensive documentation, including residual solvents and elemental impurity data, is high. Through 2035, the growth of biosimilars and the expansion of biomanufacturing capacity in emerging markets will sustain demand. Key demand-side indicators include the number of approved biologics, bioprocessing capacity utilization rates, and the adoption rate of single-use technologies.
Major companies in this segment include Dow, Wacker Chemie, and Elkem, which supply silicone-based and non-silicone defoamers tailored for bioprocessing. Current trend: Dominant and growing, driven by intensified cell culture and single-use bioreactors.
Major trends:
Adoption of single-use bioreactors increases demand for pre-qualified, ready-to-use defoamer formulations, Intensified cell culture processes (fed-batch, perfusion) raise foam control requirements, Shift toward continuous manufacturing requires reliable, long-duration foam control, Growing demand for non-silicone defoamers in protein purification workflows, and Expansion of biomanufacturing capacity in Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
Representative participants:
Dow Inc, Wacker Chemie AG, Elkem ASA, Shin-Etsu Chemical Co., Ltd, and Evonik Industries AG.
Cell and Gene Therapy Workflows (estimated share: 15%)
Cell and gene therapy workflows are emerging as a significant end-use segment for pharmaceutical defoamers, accounting for approximately 15% of global demand. These therapies involve the cultivation of sensitive cells, such as CAR-T cells and stem cells, which require carefully controlled environments. Foam formation during cell culture can damage cells and reduce viability, making effective foam control essential. However, traditional silicone-based defoamers may interfere with cell membranes or downstream purification steps, such as chromatography, leading to a preference for non-silicone alternatives like polyether-based or fatty-acid ester defoamers.
The demand for defoamers in this segment is driven by the increasing number of approved cell and gene therapies, the expansion of clinical trials, and the growing investment in manufacturing capacity for personalized medicines. Through 2035, the segment is expected to grow at a faster rate than the overall market, as more therapies reach commercialization and manufacturing processes scale up. Key demand-side indicators include the number of approved cell and gene therapies, the capacity of CDMOs specializing in these modalities, and the development of automated manufacturing platforms. Major companies supplying defoamers for this segment include BASF, Evonik, and Munzing Chemie, which offer low-toxicity, high-purity formulations.
Current trend: Fast-growing segment with demand for low-toxicity, non-interfering defoamers.
Major trends:
Increasing number of approved cell and gene therapies drives demand for specialized defoamers, Preference for non-silicone defoamers to avoid interference with cell viability and purification, Growth of automated and closed-system manufacturing platforms requires consistent foam control, Rising investment in CDMO capacity for cell and gene therapies, and Development of novel defoamer formulations with enhanced biocompatibility.
Representative participants:
BASF SE, Evonik Industries AG, Munzing Chemie GmbH, Dow Inc, and Wacker Chemie AG.
Research and Development (estimated share: 10%)
Research and development activities in the pharmaceutical industry represent about 10% of global defoamer demand. This segment includes the use of defoamers in laboratory-scale fermentation, cell culture experiments, and formulation development. During early-stage bioprocess development, researchers screen different defoamer types and concentrations to optimize cell growth and product yield. The demand for defoamers in R&D is driven by the need for reliable and reproducible results, as well as the exploration of novel drug modalities such as mRNA, viral vectors, and bispecific antibodies. Additionally, defoamers are used in analytical method development and stability studies, where foam can interfere with measurements.
The trend toward high-throughput screening and automated bioprocess development is increasing the demand for ready-to-use defoamer solutions that can be easily integrated into robotic platforms. Through 2035, R&D spending in biopharmaceuticals is expected to grow, particularly in emerging areas like personalized medicine and gene editing, supporting steady demand. Key demand-side indicators include R&D expenditure by pharmaceutical companies, the number of clinical trials, and the adoption of high-throughput screening technologies. Major suppliers to the R&D segment include Sigma-Aldrich (Merck), Thermo Fisher Scientific, and other reagent providers, as well as specialty defoamer manufacturers.
Current trend: Steady demand from bioprocess development and formulation screening.
Major trends:
High-throughput screening increases demand for ready-to-use defoamer solutions, Exploration of novel drug modalities expands the application of defoamers in R&D, Automation of bioprocess development requires consistent and reliable defoamer performance, Growing focus on formulation development for complex biologics, and Collaboration between defoamer suppliers and research institutions to develop customized solutions.
Representative participants:
Merck KGaA, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc, Dow Inc, Evonik Industries AG, and Wacker Chemie AG.
Quality Control and Release Testing (estimated share: 6%)
Quality control and release testing applications account for approximately 6% of pharmaceutical defoamer demand. Defoamers are used in analytical methods to prevent foam formation during sample preparation, dissolution testing, and chromatography, ensuring accurate and reproducible results. The demand in this segment is driven by the increasing stringency of regulatory requirements, such as ICH Q3D and USP , which mandate comprehensive testing of process aids and their potential extractables and leachables. As a result, pharmaceutical companies and contract testing laboratories require high-purity defoamers with well-characterized impurity profiles.
The growth of biologics and biosimilars, which require extensive quality control testing, is also supporting demand. Through 2035, the segment is expected to grow moderately, in line with the overall pharmaceutical quality control market. Key demand-side indicators include the number of analytical tests performed, the adoption of automated testing platforms, and the stringency of regulatory guidelines. Major suppliers include specialty chemical companies that provide analytical-grade defoamers, such as MilliporeSigma, VWR (Avantor), and others. Current trend: Moderate growth driven by regulatory requirements for analytical validation.
Major trends:
Increasing regulatory scrutiny on extractables and leachables drives demand for high-purity defoamers, Growth of biologics and biosimilars increases the volume of quality control testing, Adoption of automated analytical platforms requires consistent defoamer performance, Development of defoamers specifically designed for analytical applications, and Outsourcing of quality control testing to contract laboratories boosts demand.
Representative participants:
Merck KGaA, Avantor, Inc, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc, Dow Inc, and Wacker Chemie AG.
Other Pharmaceutical Applications (estimated share: 4%)
Other pharmaceutical applications account for the remaining 4% of defoamer demand, encompassing uses such as defoamers as excipients in liquid formulations, cleaning validation processes, and equipment maintenance. In some oral or topical formulations, defoamers are added to prevent foaming during manufacturing or to improve product stability. Cleaning validation requires defoamers that are effective in removing foam from equipment surfaces without leaving residues that could interfere with subsequent batches. The demand in this segment is driven by the need for high-quality, GMP-compliant defoamers that meet strict purity and safety standards.
Through 2035, this segment is expected to grow slowly, in line with overall pharmaceutical production. Key demand-side indicators include the number of new drug approvals, the complexity of manufacturing processes, and the adoption of single-use technologies that may reduce cleaning requirements. Major suppliers include specialty chemical companies that offer pharmaceutical-grade defoamers for diverse applications. Current trend: Niche applications including formulation excipients and cleaning validation.
Major trends:
Use of defoamers as excipients in liquid formulations to prevent foaming during manufacturing, Increasing focus on cleaning validation to ensure no residual defoamer contamination, Adoption of single-use technologies reduces cleaning requirements but may require compatible defoamers, Development of multifunctional defoamers with additional benefits, such as wetting or dispersing, and Growing demand for high-purity defoamers in sterile manufacturing environments.
Representative participants:
Dow Inc, Wacker Chemie AG, Evonik Industries AG, BASF SE, and Munzing Chemie GmbH.

Regional Dynamics
Asia-Pacific (estimated share: 40%)
Asia-Pacific dominates the pharmaceutical defoamers market, driven by the expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing in China, India, and Southeast Asia. India's FDA-inspected facilities are capturing export-oriented demand, while China's growing biologics sector fuels domestic consumption. The region benefits from lower production costs and increasing regulatory alignment with global standards. Direction: Fastest-growing region.
North America (estimated share: 30%)
North America remains a key market, supported by a strong biopharmaceutical industry and early adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies. The presence of major CDMOs and innovative biotech firms drives demand for high-quality, GMP-compliant defoamers. Regulatory focus on extractables and leachables favors suppliers with robust analytical capabilities. Direction: Steady growth.
Europe (estimated share: 20%)
Europe's pharmaceutical defoamers market is mature but growing steadily, driven by the expansion of biologics manufacturing and increasing outsourcing to CDMOs. Stringent regulatory requirements, including EMA guidelines, support demand for well-documented, high-purity defoamers. The region also sees growing interest in non-silicone alternatives for sensitive applications. Direction: Moderate growth.
Latin America (estimated share: 6%)
Latin America is an emerging market for pharmaceutical defoamers, with growth driven by increasing local biopharmaceutical production and rising healthcare investment. Brazil and Mexico are key markets, but the region faces challenges related to regulatory harmonization and infrastructure. Demand is expected to grow as local manufacturers adopt global quality standards. Direction: Emerging growth.
Middle East & Africa (estimated share: 4%)
The Middle East and Africa represent a small but growing market for pharmaceutical defoamers, supported by investments in healthcare infrastructure and local pharmaceutical manufacturing. The region's growth is constrained by limited biopharmaceutical capacity and regulatory complexity, but increasing partnerships with global suppliers are expected to drive gradual adoption. Direction: Slow but steady growth.

Pharma Industry.content:
Advertisement
News
|
Articles
|
August 31, 2026
MFN Program Grows to 26 Drugmakers as Nine More Commit to $19.6B in US Manufacturing
Author(s)
Nicholas Jacobus
Nine more manufacturers join the MFN program, pairing new Medicaid pricing deals with $19.6B in U.S. manufacturing investment and API reserve donations.
Advertisement
President Donald J. Trump announced nine new Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) agreements with pharmaceutical manufacturers on August 31, bringing the program's total roster to 26 companies. The administration says that group now accounts for 89% of the branded drug market,
1
a milestone with direct implications for how supply chain and market access teams plan pricing, procurement, and Medicaid formulary strategy heading into 2027.
Nine more manufacturers sign on
The newly announced participants are a group of mid-sized manufacturers:
Alcon
Astellas Pharma
BeOne Medicines
BridgeBio
CSL
Kyowa Kirin
Sun Pharma
Teva Pharmaceuticals
UCB
The products affected span a wide swath of costly and chronic therapeutic areas, including hemophilia, Parkinson's disease, macular degeneration, glaucoma, liver disease, dermatologic conditions, and multiple cancers.
1
Under the deals, every state Medicaid program gains access to MFN pricing on these companies' products, which the White House projects will translate into billions of dollars in aggregate savings.
1
A companion White House fact sheet frames the agreements as closing off the ability of other countries to use price controls to benefit from American drug innovation without paying comparable prices.
1
Manufacturing and supply chain commitments take center stage
For supply chain and commercialization leaders, the more consequential piece may be what's attached to the pricing deals rather than the pricing itself. The nine companies have collectively pledged at least $19.6 billion in near-term U.S. manufacturing investment, and several are directing material toward the Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Reserve, a stockpile meant to reduce dependence on foreign API sources and buffer against future supply disruptions.
1
Individual contributions include:
UCB: 163 tons of levetiracetam, an anticonvulsant
Sun Pharma: 71.4 tons of clindamycin and 6.75 tons of doxycycline, both antibiotics
Teva Pharmaceuticals: 45 metric tons of metronidazole (antibiotic/antiprotozoal) and 4.8 tons of amlodipine (antihypertensive)
Astellas: 25 kg of tacrolimus, an immunosuppressant used in transplant care
For sourcing and procurement teams, these donations are worth tracking as an early signal of how manufacturers may reallocate API supply commitments going forward.
What it means for market access
The Medicaid provisions are the piece most relevant to market access and payer-strategy teams, though industry watchers caution the practical effect on patients may be limited. Lindsay Bealor Greenleaf, head of market access policy strategy at ADVI, t
old our sister publication
Pharmaceutical Executiv
e
that Medicaid patients typically already pay only $4 to $8 out of pocket, and that the financial impact of the voluntary deals falls on manufacturers rather than patients. That distinction matters for commercialization planners weighing how MFN participation will affect net pricing and rebate structures rather than front-line patient access.
The road to 26 agreements
The nine deals build on momentum going back to May 2025, when the MFN executive order was signed, followed two months later by letters sent to 17 major manufacturers directing them to bring U.S. list prices in line with the lowest price charged in other developed markets.
2
According to the White House, all 17 of those companies have since signed on.
1
Combined with today's additions, the MFN roster now includes Pfizer, AstraZeneca, EMD Serono, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Amgen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Boehringer Ingelheim, Genentech, Gilead Sciences, GSK, Merck, Novartis, Sanofi, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Regeneron, Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals, and UCB.
1
What remains undone
Even with 26 manufacturers now committed, the administration is pushing Congress to pass the Great Healthcare Plan, broader legislation aimed at lowering drug prices and insurance premiums, increasing accountability for insurers, and expanding price transparency.
3
Unlike the manufacturer-by-manufacturer MFN deals, that agenda depends on legislative action, meaning its outcome, and any further supply chain or market access implications, rests with lawmakers rather than executive negotiation.
References
1. Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Announces Deal with Nine Additional Pharmaceutical Manufacturers to Lower Drug Prices for Americans, The White House, August 31, 2026.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Sun Pharma signs US drug pricing deal, secures tariff relief for 2 years - TradingView
Pharma Industry.content:
Sun Pharmaceutical Industries has agreed to extend "most favoured nation" (MFN) drug pricing to US state Medicaid programmes and future innovative medicine launches in exchange for a delay in impending American tariffs, India's largest drugmaker said on September 1.
The announcement came during a White House signing ceremony attended by several pharmaceutical manufacturers.
Because most details of the agreement remain confidential, the immediate financial impact on the drugmaker is difficult to quantify.
"We are proud to play our part in delivering the medicines that millions of American patients count on every day," said Rick Ascroft, North America CEO of Sun Pharma, who represented the company at the White House ceremony.
Sun Pharma said the agreement recognises company's investment in the US market by delaying Section 232 tariffs on innovative pharmaceutical products for over two years.
MFN pricing involves a pharmaceutical company voluntarily agreeing to sell a drug to US government health programmes at prices comparable to the lowest paid in other developed countries.
US President Donald Trump has threatened 100 percent tariff on imported branded pharmaceutical products and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), arguing that Americans pay far more for medicines than patients in other developed countries.
The agreement comes as Trump administration seeks to bring down prescription drug costs while simultaneously encouraging pharmaceutical investment in America.
While previous attempts to impose MFN pricing through regulation faced legal and political hurdles, the White House now appears to be pursuing voluntary agreements with manufacturers.
Why Sun Pharma signed on?
For Sun Pharma, the US is too important to ignore.
The company said the US generates roughly 27 percent of its global revenue and is its largest market for innovative medicines.
Over the past decade, Sun Pharma has evolved from being primarily a generic-drug supplier into a specialty pharmaceutical company with growing franchises in dermatology, immunology, ophthalmology and oncology.
The agreement's most notable benefit for the company is the delay of potential Section 232 tariffs on innovative pharmaceutical products for more than two years.
Section 232 refers to a US national security provision that can be used to impose tariffs on imported goods, including medicines. Such tariffs have been a major concern for the pharmaceutical industry because of their potential to disrupt supply chains and increase costs.
For Sun Pharma, avoiding tariffs may be worth more than the near-term revenue impact of extending MFN pricing, especially given its ambitions to deepen its US footprint.
The timing is notable. Earlier this year, Sun Pharma announced a definitive agreement to acquire Organon & Co in a deal valued at $11.75 billion, one of the largest acquisitions in the company's history.
The transaction underscores Sun Pharma's desire to expand its presence in the US healthcare market and build greater scale in branded medicines.
Against that backdrop, the White House agreement allows Sun Pharma to position itself as a cooperative partner in the administration's affordability agenda while safeguarding a market that is central to its future growth.
MFN programme
Sun Pharma was among the nine companies, including Astellas Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals and UCB, to sign the deal.
The latest deals bring the total number of pharmaceutical companies with MFN agreements to 26. The Trump administration said the companies covered by the programme now account for 89 percent of the US branded drug market.
The White House said the nine companies will collectively invest at least $19.6 billion in US manufacturing in the near term. Several have also agreed to donate active pharmaceutical ingredients to the US government’s strategic reserve.
The latest deals build on agreements reached with 17 major drugmakers, including Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Amgen.

Sun Pharma Shares Fall 2% After US Drug-Pricing Deal
Sun Pharma shares fell 2.3% after the company agreed to extend MFN pricing to US state Medicaid programmes, while securing a more than two-year delay in Section 232 tariffs.
Revati Krishna
Published:
1 Sept 2026, 10:30 AM IST (1 hour ago)
Last Updated:
1 Sept 2026, 10:42 AM IST (1 hour ago)
3 min read
Share
Quick Summary
Sun Pharma Share:
Sun Pharma shares fell 2.3% to ₹1,940 on September 1 after the drugmaker agreed to extend Most Favored Nation pricing to US state Medicaid programmes and future innovative medicines, while securing a delay in Section 232 tariffs for more than two years.
Sun Pharma Share:
Sun Pharmaceutical Industries shares declined in early trade on September 1, paring gains from the previous 3 sessions after the company agreed with the US government on drug pricing and tariffs. Investors weighed potential lower realisations against the tariff relief secured under the agreement.
Sun Pharma shares fell 2.3% to ₹1,940, making the stock one of the top losers on Nifty 50. The decline followed a 3.4% gain in the previous session, snapping a three-session run during which the stock had risen about 4.5%.
Despite the decline, Sun Pharma shares had gained about 15% in 2026, while Nifty 50 was down nearly 8%. The company's market capitalisation stood at more than ₹4.76 lakh crore based on Monday's close.
As of 1 Sep, 10.33 AM
What are the key details of the US agreement?
Sun Pharma joined several pharmaceutical companies at a White House ceremony for agreements aimed at improving access to affordable medicines.
Under the agreement, Sun Pharma will:
Extend Most Favored Nation (MFN) pricing to US state Medicaid programmes.
Commit to MFN pricing for future innovative medicine launches.
Contribute 71.4 tonnes of clindamycin and 6.75 tonnes of doxycycline to the Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Reserve (SAPIR).
The remaining terms are confidential. The White House said the latest agreements take the total number of pharmaceutical manufacturers with MFN deals to 26.
READ THIS ALSO:
Milky Mist Dairy Food Q1 Results FY2027: PAT Jumps 890%
What is the potential financial impact?
The pricing commitments could weigh on realisations from covered medicines. However, Sun Pharma has not disclosed the products, pricing benchmarks or extent of affected sales, so the financial impact cannot currently be quantified.
In return, the US government has agreed to delay Section 232 tariffs on Sun Pharma's innovative pharmaceutical products for more than two years, recognising its investments in the country.
US accounts for approximately 27% of Sun Pharma's global revenue and is its largest innovative-medicines market.
Sun Pharma's expanding US presence
Sun Pharma has progressively expanded beyond its traditional US generics business into higher-value innovative and specialty medicines. Its global innovative medicines portfolio across dermatology, ophthalmology and onco-dermatology accounts for about 22% of sales.
Sun Pharma is also set to increase its US exposure following its agreement to acquire Organon & Co. at an enterprise value of $11.75 billion.
Sun Pharma said the US is a key area of investment across clinical development, sales and marketing, as well as API and finished-products manufacturing.
Conclusion: What does this mean for investors?
The immediate focus is on the potential impact of MFN pricing commitments on covered US medicines, although the financial impact remains unquantified. The more than two-year tariff delay provides relief for Sun Pharma's innovative pharmaceutical products.
Investors will be watching the medicines covered by the pricing agreement, their impact on realisations and the expanding US innovative-medicines business.

Pharma Industry.content:
Sun Pharmaceutical Industries has entered into an agreement with the US government to provide most favoured nation (MFN) drug pricing to state Medicaid programmes and future innovative medicine launches.
In return, the company will receive a delay of more than two years on possible US tariffs affecting innovative pharmaceutical products.
The agreement was announced during a White House signing ceremony attended by representatives of several pharmaceutical companies.
Sun Pharma said the arrangement recognises its investment in the US healthcare market and postpones potential Section 232 tariffs on imported innovative medicines.

US President Donald Trump Announces Upto 200 Per Cent Tariffs On Generic Drug Imports; India Pharma...
Balances pricing commitments and tariff relief
Under MFN pricing, pharmaceutical companies agree to offer medicines to US government health programmes at prices comparable to the lowest rates available in other developed markets. The financial impact of the agreement remains unclear as several details have not been disclosed.
Sun Pharma’s North America CEO Rick Ascroft said the company remains committed to supplying medicines relied upon by millions of American patients.
The agreement comes as US President Donald Trump pushes measures aimed at reducing prescription drug costs while encouraging pharmaceutical companies to expand manufacturing and investment within the country. The administration has threatened tariffs of up to 100% on imported branded medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients.
US market remains crucial
The US is Sun Pharma’s largest market, contributing around 27% of its global revenue. Over the years, the company has moved beyond its traditional generic drug business and expanded into specialty medicines across areas such as dermatology, immunology, ophthalmology and oncology.
The biggest advantage of the agreement for Sun Pharma is the postponement of possible Section 232 tariffs, which could have increased costs and disrupted pharmaceutical supply chains.
Section 232 allows the US government to impose tariffs on imports considered significant from a national security perspective. The pharmaceutical sector has been closely monitoring the policy due to concerns over its impact on medicine prices and manufacturing costs.
For Sun Pharma, the tariff relief could outweigh the potential impact of extending MFN pricing, particularly as the company continues to strengthen its presence in the US market and expand its innovative medicine portfolio.

Pharma Industry.content:
Shares of Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, India's largest drugmaker, fell as much as 2.18% to ₹1,941.50 on Tuesday, 1 September, down ₹43.30 from the previous close of ₹1,984.80. The stock opened at ₹1,963.10, which was also the intraday high, and slipped to a low of ₹1,933.40, against a 52 week range of ₹1,548 to ₹2,046.90. It trades at a trailing price to earnings multiple of about 38.5 on earnings per share of ₹50.44 and offers a dividend yield of 0.82%, with a quarterly dividend of ₹4. Volume on the counter stood at around 5.73 lakh shares.

The fall came after Sun Pharma and its subsidiary Teva joined a group of nine drugmakers at the White House to announce agreements with the Trump administration to prioritise access to affordable medicine for US patients. The deal carries both a benefit and a cost for the company, and the market appears to have focused on the pricing commitments rather than the tariff relief.
Sun Pharma's White House deal
Detail
Signatories
Sun Pharma and subsidiary Teva, among nine drugmakers
Tariff impact
Section 232 tariffs on innovative products delayed two years
Pricing commitment
Most Favored Nation pricing extended to state Medicaid
Future launches
MFN pricing committed for future innovative medicines
Industry investment
$19.6 billion in US manufacturing pledged near term
Additional step
API donations to US strategic reserves
Further terms
Not disclosed, termed confidential
On the positive side, the company said in an exchange filing on Monday night that its investment in the US market over the years will result in a delay of Section 232 tariffs on innovative pharmaceutical products for a two year period. That removes a near term threat to margins on its innovative portfolio in its most important overseas market.
The offset is on pricing. Sun Pharma said it will extend Most Favored Nation pricing to state Medicaid programmes and has committed to MFN pricing for future innovative medicine launches. The Most Favored Nation policy links the cost of a prescription medicine in the US to the lowest price paid for the same drug in other developed countries, which is designed to stop US patients paying more than buyers elsewhere. For a drugmaker, that mechanism caps pricing power on exactly the high value innovative products that carry the best margins, which is the part of the deal the market is weighing. Sun Pharma did not disclose further terms, describing them as confidential.
The scale of the US business is what makes the deal material. Sun Pharma's US presence began through the generics route before shifting toward innovative and specialty medicines. It now ranks second by prescriptions in the US dermatology segment and is expanding across dermatology, immunology, cutaneous oncology and ophthalmology. The US is its largest market for innovative medicines and, as of the June quarter, contributed 27% of the company's overall topline. The North America chief executive Rick Ascroft said the US is a key area of investment across clinical development, sales and marketing, and both active ingredient and finished product manufacturing.
The broader context is a coordinated push by the Trump administration to lower US drug prices and reshore manufacturing. According to a White House fact sheet, the nine companies that signed the pricing deal on Monday have committed to invest $19.6 billion in US manufacturing in the near term. Sun Pharma is also among the companies that have agreed to donate active pharmaceutical ingredients for key products to the government's strategic reserves, a move aimed at cutting US dependence on imports. Separately, the company has been deepening its US bets, recently announcing a definitive agreement to acquire Organon and Co at an enterprise value of $11.75 billion.
The India angle is significant. Sun Pharma is the largest Indian pharmaceutical company and a bellwether for a sector that counts the US as its single biggest export destination, so any change in US pricing and tariff policy sends signals across the entire Indian pharma space. The two year delay on Section 232 tariffs is a relief for Indian drugmakers with US exposure, but the spread of Most Favored Nation pricing raises a longer term question about how much pricing power Indian companies can retain on innovative products in their key growth market. For investors tracking the sector, the trade off visible in Sun Pharma's reaction, tariff certainty gained against pricing flexibility given up, is the template likely to apply to other India based exporters as more such deals are struck.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Trump strikes nine more deals with drugmakers to lower prices - STAT
Pharma Industry.content:
President Trump has announced another round of pricing deals with drugmakers.
Win McNamee/Getty Images
By
Daniel Payne
and
Elaine Chen
Aug. 31, 2026
Daniel Payne
[email protected]
Daniel covers the intersection of the health industry and the federal government. He reports on corporate influence in government, the health consequences of federal policies, and the politics of health care. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at danielp.100.
Elaine Chen
[email protected]
Elaine’s stories explore the boom in new obesity treatments, new drug payment models, the ways companies are affected by FDA changes, and the emerging psychedelics drug sector. She co-writes
The Readout newsletter
, and co-hosts STAT’s weekly biotech podcast,
The Readout Loud
. You can reach Elaine on Signal at elaineywchen.70.
WASHINGTON — President Trump on Monday announced the next round of pricing deals with drugmakers, with nine new companies joining the 17 that reached agreements with the administration previously.
The new companies striking deals — Alcon, Astellas, BeOne, BridgeBio, CSL, Sun Pharma, Kyowa Kirin, Teva, and UCB — made pledges similar to those made by larger drugmakers before them: to sell new medications to U.S. patients at prices comparable to the lowest prices in peer countries, to offer their drugs to state Medicaid programs at “most-favored nation” prices, and, in some instances, to bolster domestic manufacturing and contribute to the U.S. medical stockpiles. In return, it’s believed at least some of the companies will avoid tariffs.
Advertisement
UCB, Sun Pharma, Teva, and Astellas will, together, contribute 290 metric tons of active pharmaceutical ingredients to the country’s strategic reserves as part of the deals. All of the new companies except BridgeBio are headquartered outside of the U.S.
The agreements come after months of biotech and pharma companies have sought deals with the administration to avoid what they see as price controls through
Medicare pilot programs
that would have linked the cost of drugs in the U.S. to their prices in other countries. Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on Monday nine out of 10 drugs prescribed in the U.S. were now covered by the deals.
The details of the new deals, including the impact on Medicare, have not been publicly released.
Advertisement
It’s not clear what effect these agreements will have on drug costs and accessibility. Medicaid already receives the lowest drug prices out of any payer in the U.S. Additionally, two of the companies making new deals, Teva and Sun Pharma, specialize in making generic drugs.
The new deals are the latest expansion of Trump’s drug pricing agenda, which has become a centerpiece of the administration’s plans to reform American health care. In April,
administration officials promised
to work out agreements with the “many hundreds” of other drugmakers.
Kennedy said Monday that the president, through a series of “very, very emotional conversations,” made clear he and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz could lose their jobs if they didn’t deliver drug pricing deals. (“I didn’t want to fire a Kennedy,” Trump said. “I wasn’t going to do that.”)
The White House has repeatedly declined to make the details public while also pushing Congress to codify the agreements. Administration officials have
touted declines
in drug prices in the U.S., though Trump’s signature TrumpRx drug purchasing platform
has fallen short
of its grand goals.

tried, and failed
, to get company leaders to endorse its drug pricing legislation. And drugmakers are still
considering their legal options
to overturn the administration’s drug pricing policies.
Still, private sector leaders have taken officials up on voluntary, private deals
that end with this administration

Pharma Policy.url_match_title: Trump Claims Credit for Drug Price Decline. Experts Say It’s More Complicated. - FactCheck.org
Pharma Policy.content:
President Donald Trump and other administration officials are claiming credit for a recent drop in prescription drug prices, citing deals they’ve struck with drugmakers and the launch of the online direct-to-consumer platform TrumpRx. But experts are skeptical those measures have had much impact on prices overall, and they say other factors likely explain most of the decline.
Trump and his allies were quick to celebrate when the
latest consumer price data
from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, released in mid-August, showed prescription drug prices falling 3.1%
over the past year
. The data
measure
prices paid by consumers and insurers at retail, internet or mail-order pharmacies.
“Under my most-favored-nation policy on drug prices, we are delivering the largest prescription drug price cuts in the history of our country,” Trump said during
an Aug. 14 speech
on Long Island, referring to agreements with companies to offer certain drugs at prices comparable to those in other countries.
He repeated the claim during
an Aug. 31
event at the White House at which he announced deals with additional companies.
Trump announces the launch of his TrumpRx prescription drug platform on Feb. 5. Official White House photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.
Similarly, in an
interview
with CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Aug. 23, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz attributed the drop to the administration’s dealmaking and the launch of
TrumpRx
, which lists discounts on certain drugs for consumers paying cash prices.
“This increasing savings that we’re seeing, the additional amount of savings we’re getting — primarily driven not just by having the medications at most-favored-nation pricing, but available to the American people on TrumpRx.gov — is seismic in its nature,” Oz said.
Oz put it more succinctly in an
X post
two days earlier: “Why did drug prices DROP? The answer: President Donald J. Trump fulfilling his promises to the American people.”
But several drug pricing experts told us the reasons for that decline are a lot more complicated than the administration is letting on — and neither TrumpRx nor the agreements with drug companies are likely to have been major drivers.
They cited other factors they see as likely having a bigger impact, including market pressures driving down the cost of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, more generics entering the market and a Biden-era policy that allows Medicare to negotiate drug prices.
“I think it’s totally possible that there are both some Republican policies — or, you know, Trump policies — as well as Biden policies that are at play here,” Cynthia Cox, a senior vice president at the nonpartisan health policy research organization KFF, told us. “But I think there’s also just market forces at play, in particular around GLP-1 drugs, that are really hard to ignore.”
Asked about the basis for the president’s claims that his policies are driving a major reduction in drug prices, White House spokesman Kush Desai rejected the idea that Medicare price negotiations implemented during the Biden administration, which apply to 10 drugs so far, made a big difference.
“President Trump’s Most-Favored-Nations deals, on the other hand, cover hundreds of drugs, including GLP-1s and fertility drugs that are enormously popular and not typically covered by insurance,” he said in a statement. “TrumpRx.gov has already saved real patients over $700 million, and the President’s MFN policies are set to save America over $500 billion in the next 10 years.”
We’ve
previously written
about the shaky assumptions behind that $500 billion number. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services referred questions to the White House.
Effects of Drug Pricing Deals, TrumpRx ‘Murky’
It’s true that prescription drugs have just seen the largest one-year price decline in decades, as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index. The CPI tracks prescription drug prices based on what individuals and insurers, including Medicare drug plans, pay to pharmacies.
Those prices
are down
3.1% since last July, the largest one-year decrease since 1963. Prices didn’t change much in the second half of 2025, but have dropped 3.3% since the start of this year — the steepest six-month drop since the BLS started tracking prescription drug costs in 1947.
Trump and other administration officials say the drop is due to deals they’ve struck with major pharmaceutical companies to offer certain drugs at so-called “most favored nation” prices, or prices that are comparable to those in other developed countries. The U.S. tends to
pay significantly more
than other wealthy nations for brand-name drugs.
Since November, the Trump administration has announced agreements with 17 large drug companies, including
Pfizer
,
Merck
and
Johnson & Johnson
, to implement MFN pricing for certain drugs in exchange for three years of tariff relief. (The administration
announced
similar deals with nine midsize biotech companies Aug. 31.) Trump has sometimes described those deals in sweeping terms.
“For decades, Americans paid the highest prices for prescription drugs,” Trump said in his Aug. 14 speech. “We paid more for prescription drugs than anywhere in the world. And now we pay the lowest price anywhere in the world for prescription drugs.”
But as we’ve
explained
before,
the agreements
are much narrower than Trump’s description suggests.
Companies did pledge to release at least some new drugs at prices comparable to those in other wealthy nations. But for existing drugs, MFN prices apply in only limited circumstances — drugs sold to state Medicaid programs, direct-to-consumer sales through TrumpRx and certain GLP-1 weight loss and diabetes drugs sold to Medicare or Medicaid. The agreements do not affect the prices of drugs already on the market for the
majority
of Americans who use private insurance.
“Right now, the only places where those MFN prices would show up in the CPI would be through TrumpRx,” said
Jeromie Ballreich
, a health economist at Johns Hopkins University who studies pharmaceutical economics and policy. (As a measure of consumer prices, the CPI
doesn’t factor in
what Medicaid pays because it’s fully taxpayer-funded.) And he said TrumpRx is unlikely to have had major effects on the overall prescription-drug market because it serves a relatively small subset of patients. “It’s not a big factor in the market.”
TrumpRx, which the federal government launched in February, features discounts on a selection of brand-name drugs for self-pay consumers, i.e., those not using insurance. As we’ve
written before
, the site may offer savings for some patients buying certain drugs, such as those without insurance or those who need expensive medications their insurance won’t cover, including GLP-1 drugs for weight loss. But most people will get a better deal going through their insurance, and some drugs featured on the platform also have cheaper generic versions available elsewhere.
The White House says TrumpRx has already saved Americans more than $700 million, though it hasn’t released the details of how it calculated that figure. A spokesperson said it’s based on comparing what people paid when buying medications through the site to what the prior net prices would have been. Seven hundred million dollars would represent less than 0.2% of the
$467 billion
that was spent on prescription drugs in the U.S. in 2024, according to the government’s national health expenditure data.
Additionally, Ballreich said drug companies and the White House have been relatively vague about the details of the MFN deals in their public statements, so it’s unclear exactly how far-reaching they are. Some
companies’
Securities and Exchange Commission
filings
suggest that only some of their products are subject to the agreements.
“They didn’t have enough detail about, is it all new drugs?” Ballreich said. “Only some new drugs?”
Similarly,
Richard Frank
, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and director of the think tank’s Center on Health Policy, said the limited scope and lack of detail make it hard to assess the impact of these deals.
“There are an unknown, but probably small, number of drugs where there have been any negotiations with the Trump people, and it’s not even obvious that those have been implemented yet,” he said. “So all of this is kind of murky. It’s not that it’s implausible that they have some effect. But it’s really unlikely that they are the major drivers here.”
As for TrumpRx, Frank said there are still questions around its uptake and the extent of savings it actually offers.
“That’s an area where there could be a contribution,” he said. “But again, I would be surprised if it was very large.”
Cox, with KFF, said it’s possible that a newly launched
pilot program
to make reduced-price GLP-1 drugs available to certain Medicare beneficiaries factored into the most recent CPI prescription drug data, which registered a 0.8% drop in July.
The administration says Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly — the makers of Ozempic/Wegovy and Mounjaro/Zepbound, respectively — have
agreed
to provide the drugs to Medicare for $245 per month, and certain Medicare beneficiaries became eligible to access the drugs for weight loss for the first time at a $50 monthly copay, starting July 1.
“That would correspond with the timing of this particular [month’s] drop in the CPI,” Cox said, but not the declines that happened earlier this year.
Other Reasons for the Drop in Prices
Experts told us they see other factors as more likely explanations for the year-to-year drop in drug prices, though they cautioned that they don’t yet have clear empirical data on exactly what’s going on.
For one, Cox said, GLP-1 prices have been coming down for reasons other than the administration’s dealmaking, including heightened competition between drugmakers as new GLP-1s enter the market.
“There’s competition within the class, there’s competition from compound pharmacies, there’s the fact that a lot of people don’t have insurance coverage for these drugs but really want them, and so they’re paying out of pocket and price-sensitive,” she said. “And there’s this kind of pressure from insurers and employers to bring down the prices, because they might want to offer that coverage but not at the current price.”
Frank likewise pointed to competition in the GLP-1 market lowering prices for those drugs. “Since their sales have been so high, they would get quite a bit of weight in the CPI,” he said.
Another likely factor is that a number of bestselling brand-name drugs
recently lost patent protection
, Ballreich said. “So we had generics and biosimilars come on the market at cheaper prices.”
Ballreich also credits a policy signed into law by President Joe Biden as part of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, which gave Medicare the authority to negotiate prices for certain expensive drugs. The negotiated prices for the first 10 of those drugs — which were dispensed to
nearly 9 million beneficiaries
in 2023 and accounted for about 20% of Medicare prescription drug spending that year — took effect in January.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
estimated
in 2024 that the negotiated prices would have saved the program $6 billion had they been in effect for the prior year. It also projected that beneficiaries would save around $1.5 billion in out-of-pocket costs on those drugs in 2026 because of the lower prices.
“For Trump to take credit in drug pricing, I do think one of the biggest things he did was he did not dismantle Medicare price negotiations,” Ballreich said.
Frank is less confident that the initial batch of Medicare price negotiations was a major driver of the decline in overall prescription drug costs. He views it as possible but unlikely, given the negotiations involved a relatively small, if costly, set of medications. Some of the impact would depend on how much those particular drugs are weighted in the CPI index, he said.
“On the Medicare side, there are 10 drugs. They were generally relatively big sellers,” he said. But as with Trump’s MFN deals, “we don’t know how quickly they’ve all worked their way through the supply chain.”
Frank said other possible factors could be in the mix as well. Pharmacy benefit managers — the third-party companies that manage prescription drug benefits for insurers — have been under
pressure
to pass on more of the savings from rebates they negotiate with drug companies. He also said that we don’t know how a separate provision of the IRA — the
Inflation Rebate Program
, which aims to discourage drugmakers from raising their prices too fast — may have affected prices.
“There are a lot of moving parts here,” he said. “It would be surprising to me if the administration’s MFN negotiations played a big part of it, just like I wouldn’t have guessed that the IRA negotiations played a huge part of it.”
In his statement, Desai, the White House spokesman, called the idea that the Medicare price negotiations had made a big difference in the CPI “absolutely idiotic and unfounded.”
“The so-called Inflation ‘Reduction’ Act negotiated prices just on Medicare for a whopping 10 drugs, and failed to deliver any meaningful price reductions beyond discounts that private insurers had already negotiated,” he said. “These discounts came into effect in January 2026 without making a dent in the prescription drug CPI for February 2026.”
The CPI’s prescription drug index dropped about 0.2% in February before registering a bigger decline of 1.5% in March.
Whether people notice a difference in what they’re actually paying at the pharmacy, of course, generally has more to do with the specific features of their insurance plan, Ballreich said. “That will have a much more influential effect on them as patients, rather than general drug pricing trends.”

President Trump has announced another round of pricing deals with drugmakers.
Win McNamee/Getty Images
By
Daniel Payne
and

Daniel Payne

Daniel covers the intersection of the health industry and the federal government. He reports on corporate influence in government, the health consequences of federal policies, and the politics of health care. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at danielp.100.
Elaine Chen

Elaine’s stories explore the boom in new obesity treatments, new drug payment models, the ways companies are affected by FDA changes, and the emerging psychedelics drug sector. She co-writes
The Readout newsletter
, and co-hosts STAT’s weekly biotech podcast,
The Readout Loud
. You can reach Elaine on Signal at elaineywchen.70.
WASHINGTON — President Trump on Monday announced the next round of pricing deals with drugmakers, with nine new companies joining the 17 that reached agreements with the administration previously.
The new companies striking deals — Alcon, Astellas, BeOne, BridgeBio, CSL, Sun Pharma, Kyowa Kirin, Teva, and UCB — made pledges similar to those made by larger drugmakers before them: to sell new medications to U.S. patients at prices comparable to the lowest prices in peer countries, to offer their drugs to state Medicaid programs at “most-favored nation” prices, and, in some instances, to bolster domestic manufacturing and contribute to the U.S. medical stockpiles. In return, it’s believed at least some of the companies will avoid tariffs.
Advertisement
UCB, Sun Pharma, Teva, and Astellas will, together, contribute 290 metric tons of active pharmaceutical ingredients to the country’s strategic reserves as part of the deals. All of the new companies except BridgeBio are headquartered outside of the U.S.
The agreements come after months of biotech and pharma companies have sought deals with the administration to avoid what they see as price controls through
Medicare pilot programs
that would have linked the cost of drugs in the U.S. to their prices in other countries. Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on Monday nine out of 10 drugs prescribed in the U.S. were now covered by the deals.
The details of the new deals, including the impact on Medicare, have not been publicly released.
Advertisement
It’s not clear what effect these agreements will have on drug costs and accessibility. Medicaid already receives the lowest drug prices out of any payer in the U.S. Additionally, two of the companies making new deals, Teva and Sun Pharma, specialize in making generic drugs.
The new deals are the latest expansion of Trump’s drug pricing agenda, which has become a centerpiece of the administration’s plans to reform American health care. In April,
administration officials promised
to work out agreements with the “many hundreds” of other drugmakers.
Kennedy said Monday that the president, through a series of “very, very emotional conversations,” made clear he and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz could lose their jobs if they didn’t deliver drug pricing deals. (“I didn’t want to fire a Kennedy,” Trump said. “I wasn’t going to do that.”)
The White House has repeatedly declined to make the details public while also pushing Congress to codify the agreements. Administration officials have
touted declines
in drug prices in the U.S., though Trump’s signature TrumpRx drug purchasing platform
has fallen short
of its grand goals.
The voluntary agreements do not mean drugmakers are in full agreement with the administration’s aims. Officials have
tried, and failed
, to get company leaders to endorse its drug pricing legislation. And drugmakers are still
considering their legal options
to overturn the administration’s drug pricing policies.
Still, private sector leaders have taken officials up on voluntary, private deals
that end with this administration
.

Evelyn Hockstein | Reuters
President
Donald Trump
on Monday said he struck new drug pricing deals with nine drugmakers to voluntarily sell their medications for less, building on his push to
link the nation's pharmaceutical prices
to cheaper ones abroad.
The drugmakers signing the new deals are Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals and UCB, according to the White House. Shares of most of those companies closed relatively flat on Monday, while Teva and BeOne fell around 1%.
Under the new deals, the nine companies agreed to provide discounts on outpatient drugs to every state Medicaid program so that prices states pay align with what companies charge in foreign countries. The agreements impact drugs that treat several chronic and rare diseases, such as hemophilia, liver disease, skin conditions and certain forms of cancer.
The companies committed to invest at least $19.6 billion collectively in U.S. manufacturing in the near term, according to the White House.
Astellas, Sun Pharma, Teva and UCB also agreed to donate active pharmaceutical ingredients for key products to the federal government's strategic reserve of those ingredients, which aims to reduce reliance on foreign supply and ensure the U.S. is prepared in the event of an emergency. For example, UCB will contribute 163 tons of levetiracetam, an anticonvulsant used to control and prevent certain types of seizures.
The new agreements bring the Trump administration's total number of drug pricing deals to 26 companies, which the president said represents 90% of the domestic pharmaceutical market. He said the other 10% of the industry is "also coming in" and "have no choice."
Over the past year, the Trump administration reached drug pricing deals with 17 other pharmaceutical companies, including
Pfizer
,
Eli Lilly
and
Novo Nordisk
, as part of its "most favored nation" policy. Trump signed an
executive order
in May 2025 to revive that policy, calling for prices to be increased outside of the U.S. and to "end global freeloading."
The deals add to the White House's efforts to spotlight healthcare affordability ahead of the midterm elections.
The "most favored nation" deals that have been signed with the Trump administration have already impacted the commercial strategies, bottom lines and manufacturing pipelines of major pharmaceutical companies.
To insulate themselves from future tariff threats, drugmakers are spending billions of dollars to bring manufacturing capabilities back to the U.S. Companies are also drastically expanding direct-to-consumer channels for their products, including by offering their medicines on the president's
TrumpRx portal
. Lower prices in the U.S. are weighing on bottom lines, with manufacturers like Novo Nordisk saying that it will take time for
prescription volumes to offset
the revenue dip.
U.S. prescription drug prices on average are
nearly three times higher
than they are overseas, according to a 2024 study by Rand Corp. Prices for branded drugs were more than four times higher, the report found.
The trade association PhRMA, which represents many major pharma companies, has previously said that most-favored nation pricing
isn't the best way to lower drug costs
for Americans and instead blamed pharmacy benefit managers for the price disparity.
The U.S. is the single most important market for many drugmakers, regardless of their home country. Despite being based across the Atlantic, European pharma companies are heavily exposed to the U.S. market, with half of the 10 largest companies on the continent generating a
majority of their sales in the U.S.

Pharma Policy.content:
Jessica Corbett
Jessica Corbett is a senior editor and staff writer for Common Dreams.
US President
Donald Trump
on Monday announced nine more agreements with pharmaceutical manufacturers intended to lower prescription
drug prices
nationwide, bringing the total to 26, but patient advocates responded skeptically.
The administration previously struck "most favored nation" (MFN) deals with 17 large drug manufacturers. The new ones with midsized companies—Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals, and UCB—mean that 89% of the branded drug market is subject to an agreement,
according to
a
White House
fact sheet.
"It has been nearly a year since Trump
announced his first
secret MFN deal with Pfizer, and he has almost nothing to show for it," Peter Maybarduk, Access to Medicines director at the watchdog group
Public Citizen
,
said
in a Monday statement. "The new deals are a distraction from the administration's failed plan to lower US drug prices to the levels paid in other wealthy countries."
Earlier this month, Public Citizen
released
an analysis of Trump's policies to cut drug costs, including MFN deals. Maybarduk said at the time that "Trump has three kinds of drug pricing policy: fake, exaggerated, and not-real-yet, probably-won't-happen."
Following Monday's agreements, the campaigner argued that "a more serious approach would build international reference pricing into
Medicare
drug price negotiation. Instead, Trump is cozying up to
Big Pharma
and keeping American drug prices high."
"There still is no evidence that any pharma company has followed through on prior commitments to the
Trump administration
to launch new drugs at MFN price points," he explained. "Uptake of TrumpRx, which may cause consumers to overpay on medicines,
has been lackluster
."
TrumpRx is a government-operated website that helps patients find discounted prices and coupons for certain medications—and, as the Public Citizen analysis highlighted, the only part of the president's MFN program that is fully underway.
"The Centers for Medicare and
Medicaid
Services (CMS) has not announced any state participants in a pilot to test MFN-based prices in Medicaid," Maybarduk noted. "And CMS has failed to issue final rules to test MFN-pricing in Medicare, while simultaneously
excluding
almost all drug companies from these programs."
Public Citizen said it plans to immediately file a Freedom of Information Act request to obtain the texts of these "farce" deals—a pledge that came just days after US Sen.
Elizabeth Warren
(D-Mass.)
highlighted
that
Health and Human Services
Secretary
Robert F. Kennedy Jr
. has failed to publicize initial 17 agreements, despite agreeing to do so during an April hearing.
Like Public Citizen, the advocacy group Patients for Affordable Drugs was critical of the new deals, with CEO Merith Basey pointing out that "for decades, drug companies have been charging Americans at least four times more for brand-name medicines than people in other high-income nations."
"Patients need systemic reforms that will lower drug prices, rather than short-term, voluntary agreements whose terms remain secret," she asserted. "The deals announced today focus on Medicaid, where steep discounts already exist, and even then, states can choose whether to participate. Lasting relief requires transparent, enforceable measures that lower drug prices and hold big drug companies accountable."
As the industry
trade
publication Fierce Pharma
reported
, the large companies behind the initial deals "made a combination of drug pricing commitments and domestic investment pledges to win temporary immunity from the Trump administration's
drug import tariffs
," and "individual company press releases Monday, like UCB's, suggest that
tariff immunity
is still very much part of the MFN equation."
Although Trump's tried taking credit for a recent drop in medication costs, with the White House X account
claiming
Monday that he's "leveled the playing field, and made prescription drugs more affordable than ever for the American people," as Common Dreams
reported
earlier this month, experts have cited the Biden administration's policy allowing
Medicare
to directly negotiate some prices.
As Trump has touted his MFN deals, critics of the
United States
' for-profit
healthcare
system have in recent months renewed calls for shifting to Medicare for All—which new research
shows
would save over 114,000 lives and $1 trillion each year—and other healthcare
reforms
, including breaking up industry giants, capping drug prices, strengthening
antitrust
enforcement, and expanding the sector's workforce.

Trump Administration Targets Medicaid Drug Pricing Reform
The Trump administration's new plan aims to lower drug prices for Medicaid recipients, altering pricing strategy for pharmaceuticals.
The Trump administration has announced a significant shift in its approach to drug pricing for the Medicaid programme, which provides healthcare for low-income individuals and families in the United States. Under the new plan, pharmaceutical companies will see changes in how their products are priced for these vulnerable populations.
This policy initiative is designed to reduce expenditures on prescription medications, as the administration seeks to align pricing structures more closely with market realities. A key aspect of the reform is the introduction of a revised pricing model that aims to offer better access to essential medications at lower costs.
While the details of the plan are still being formulated, officials have indicated that it will primarily focus on negotiated pricing strategies. This means that Medicaid, which is jointly funded by state and federal governments, will have more authority in determining the prices it pays for drugs.
Supporters of the reform argue that it is a necessary step to ensure that low-income individuals have access to affordable medications. By re-evaluating the pricing landscape, the administration hopes to place downward pressure on the rising costs of pharmaceuticals, which have been a source of concern for many healthcare advocates.
However, critics have raised concerns about potential implications for pharmaceutical innovation. Some industry experts argue that reduced revenues may hinder companies' ability to invest in research and development for new drugs, which could have long-term consequences for healthcare advancements.
The new policy comes amidst ongoing debates over healthcare reform in the United States. The administration's intent is clear: to address the escalating costs of drugs that have burdened healthcare systems and those who rely on Medicaid for their medical needs.
As the administration prepares to roll out the specific details of the reform, it will be essential to monitor its impacts on both pricing and access to medications for millions of Americans enrolled in Medicaid.
