Pharma Policy.content:
For over 30 years, I stood behind a pharmacy counter and watched hardworking neighbors open their mouths in disbelief when I told them what their
prescriptions
would cost. I watched them ask if there was a less expensive generic, or if they could stretch a 30-day supply into 45 days, or simply walk out without the medication their
doctor
prescribed.
For decades, Washington talked about lowering drug prices, but nothing changed. President
Donald Trump
has finally changed course.
Recommended Stories
From $1,000 to $149: Trump just unlocked the biggest drug price drop in 60 years
This beauty queen might be one of Israel’s most effective diplomats
Florida Republicans just delivered on a Democrat’s decades-old environmental promise
He walked into a fight that previous administrations had avoided for a generation, and instead of another round of congressional hearings and strongly worded letters, he used the leverage of the presidency to force an industry that had never once lowered its prices voluntarily to do exactly that.
Advertisement
New government data show that Trump has delivered the largest drop in prescription drug prices in over 60 years. Prices have fallen every single month this year. No previous administration, Republican or Democrat, has managed to bend the cost curve downward on prescription drugs as this president has.
Trump made this happen by doing what no one else in Washington was willing to do: stand up to an industry that has spent decades charging Americans far more than it charges patients anywhere else in the world. His administration struck landmark agreements with major drug manufacturers requiring them to bring fairer, more competitive prices to American patients, and he backed that demand with the leverage to make it stick. Just this week, that momentum grew even further: Trump announced
nine more drugmakers
, including Teva, Sun Pharma, and CSL, have agreed to cut prices for patients, bringing the total to 26 companies representing 89% of the branded American
pharmaceutical market
.
The clearest proof of his success is TrumpRx, the new platform the administration built so Americans can shop for their medications directly and see real prices before purchasing. What began earlier this year with a handful of manufacturers has already grown to more than 800 medications. GLP-1 drugs that previously cost over $1,000 a month are now available for as little as $149. The Department of Veterans Affairs alone has locked in a record $10 billion in pharmaceutical savings this fiscal year, savings that go straight back to caring for the veterans who earned them.
Advertisement
Trump has built the momentum. His administration has proven that meaningful drug price relief is not just possible, it is already happening.
Congress
now has a real opportunity to build on that progress and make these gains last, starting with reining in pharmacy benefit managers, the shadowy middlemen who profit from confusion in our system by placing their own bottom line ahead of the patient’s health.
As vice chairwoman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee’s Health Subcommittee, I have spent much of my time in Congress fighting that battle. That’s why I introduced my bipartisan Patients Before Monopolies Act to ban the kind of joint ownership between PBMs and pharmacies that lets a single company set the price, fill the prescription, and pocket the markup, the exact self-dealing arrangement that has driven independent pharmacies out of business and driven costs up for the patients they claim to serve.
OPINION: YOUR DOCTOR HAS TO BEG AI FOR PERMISSION TO SAVE YOUR LIFE
Advertisement
Trump’s work to force fairer prices from drug manufacturers and my work to rein in the middlemen who mark them up are aimed at the same target: a system where the shelf price reflects the value of the medication, not who has the most leverage in the supply chain.
I know what it looks like when a patient cannot afford to fill a prescription. I also know what it looks like when they finally can. The president has proven that real relief is possible, and that progress deserves to outlast any single administration. It is time for Congress to build on what Trump started and make sure that promise continues to be kept.
Rep. Diana Harshbarger is a Republican representing Tennessee’s First Congressional District and serves as vice chairwoman of the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health. She spent 30 years as a licensed community pharmacist in East Tennessee before her election to Congress and is still a licensed pharmacist.

McDermottPlus LLC was hired as a lobbying firm for
Patients for Affordable Drugs Now Inc.
Loper Consulting LLC had been working with Patients for Affordable Drugs Now Inc. since the first quarter of 2018.
Broader Context
The client's lobbying agenda during that period focused on several fronts. In the first quarter of 2021, the group pushed for continued monitoring of implementation of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act. In 2021, Patients for Affordable Drugs Now Inc. lobbied on prescription drug pricing issues. The organization then tracked specific legislative vehicles, including S. 2210, the Better Care Better Jobs Act, in the third quarter, and S. 610, the Protecting Medicare and American Farmers from Sequester Cuts Act, in the fourth quarter.
However, the engagement with Loper Consulting represented a consistent client relationship over at least a full year.

, a Vice President at McDermottPlus LLC, previously worked for Rep. Charles Norwood (R-GA-10).
Amy Kelbick
, a Senior Director of Health Policy at McDermottPlus LLC, previously worked for Rep. Bill Foster (D-IL-11).
Debbie Curtis
, a Principal at McDermottPlus LLC, served as a lobbyist for Patients for Affordable Drugs Now Inc. and previously worked for Rep. Fortney Pete Stark (D-CA-13). Julia Grabo, a Manager at McDermottPlus LLC, has prior experience as staff for Rep. Colin Z. Allred (D-TX-32).
Josh Jorgensen
, a Director at the firm, also brings congressional experience from his time in the
114th through 116th Congresses
.
The Bottom Line
McDermottPlus LLC represented Patients for Affordable Drugs Now Inc. on prescription drug competition and pricing issues and pharmacy benefit management reform issues.

Pharma Policy.content:
Trump Strikes 'Lowest-Price' Drug Deals with 9 Mid-Sized Pharma Firms, Securing $19.6 Billion in US Investment
Add to Google Preferred Sources
The Trump administration has signed Most Favored Nation (MFN) drug pricing agreements with nine mid-sized pharmaceutical companies, including Alcon, Astellas, Teva, UCB, and Sun Pharma. In exchange for lowering US prescription drug prices to the lowest levels paid by other developed nations, these companies have committed to investing more than $19.6 billion in US manufacturing facilities and donating critical active pharmaceutical ingredients to the strategic national stockpile. The agreements bring the total number of pharmaceutical companies under MFN deals to 26, representing 89% of the US branded drug market. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates approximately $600 billion in cost savings over the next decade. Shares of the publicly traded companies involved showed little movement immediately following the announcement.
Key Elements
Donald Trump
White House
Teva Pharmaceutical
UCB
Sun Pharma
Astellas Pharma
Kyowa Kirin
CSL
MFN Drug Pricing Agreement
Medicaid
Alcon
BeOne Medicines
BridgeBio
The US government has partnered with nine global mid-sized pharmaceutical companies to lower prescription drug prices to the lowest levels paid by other developed nations, in exchange for securing $19.6 billion (approximately 26.8 trillion won) in US manufacturing investment from these firms. The Trump administration's strategy of pursuing both drug price reductions and supply chain reshoring is now extending to mid-sized pharmaceutical companies.
The White House announced on the 31st (local time) that it had signed new Most Favored Nation (MFN) drug pricing agreements with nine companies: Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceutical, and UCB. MFN is a policy that aligns US prescription drug prices with the lowest prices paid by other wealthy nations, and has been a cornerstone of the Trump administration's drug pricing policy since last year.
According to a report released on the 1st by the Korea Bio Association's Bio Economy Research Center, state Medicaid programs across the US will now receive MFN pricing on drugs produced by these nine companies. The targeted disease areas include hemophilia, Parkinson's disease, macular degeneration, glaucoma, liver disease, skin conditions, and various cancers—chronic and rare diseases with high treatment costs. The White House plans to apply the same MFN pricing to innovative new drugs these companies launch in the future, reducing the drug cost burden on American patients.
With this agreement, the total number of pharmaceutical companies under MFN deals with the Trump administration has grown to 26. The nine new companies join the existing 17 large pharmaceutical firms that previously reached agreements, including Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Amgen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Gilead, GSK, Merck, Novartis, Sanofi, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, and Regeneron. These companies now account for 89% of the US branded drug market. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates that the MFN policy will generate approximately $600 billion (about 820.9 trillion won) in cost savings over the next decade.
In exchange for lower drug prices, the pharmaceutical companies are committing substantial capital to strengthen US production and supply chains. The nine companies participating in this agreement have pledged to invest a total of more than $19.6 billion in US manufacturing facilities in the near term—approximately 26.8 trillion won.
Stockpiling of critical active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) in the US is also expanding. UCB plans to donate 163 tons of the anticonvulsant levetiracetam to the US Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Reserve (SAPIR). Sun Pharma will provide 71.4 tons of the antibiotic clindamycin and 6.75 tons of doxycycline, while Teva will supply 45 tons of metronidazole and 4.8 tons of the hypertension drug amlodipine. Astellas will also donate 25 kilograms of tacrolimus, used to prevent rejection in organ transplant patients, to the stockpile.
This signals that drug pricing policy is evolving beyond simply reducing patient medication costs and is now being combined with a US-centric pharmaceutical supply chain restructuring strategy. While global pharmaceutical companies have been expanding their US manufacturing facilities recently, the critical stages of API production remain concentrated overseas, particularly in China and India. This is the backdrop for the US government's move to manage not just finished drug production but also APIs as strategic assets.
Industry observers believe tariff considerations played a significant role in these companies' decisions to participate. The White House did not disclose specific incentives or tariff benefits offered to the pharmaceutical companies in this announcement, but trade tariffs have served as a key negotiating tool in previous MFN negotiations. In fact, announcements from some companies, including UCB, suggest that tariff exemptions were a major factor in the MFN negotiations.
Notably, unlike previous MFN agreements dominated by large American and European pharmaceutical companies, this round includes India's Sun Pharma, Israel's Teva, Japan's Astellas and Kyowa Kirin, and Australia's CSL. Observers say the Trump administration's pressure for drug price reductions and expanded US production is now spreading in earnest to global mid-sized pharmaceutical companies.
Shares of the publicly traded companies involved showed little movement immediately following the announcement. Teva closed down 1.1% in regular trading before rising 2% in after-hours trading. BeOne Medicines held at a decline of about 2%, while BridgeBio was nearly flat in regular trading before ticking up slightly after hours. Alcon also showed little change. Year-to-date, Teva is up 16% and BeOne Medicines up 18%, while Alcon is down 9% and BridgeBio remains near flat.
This agreement demonstrates that the Trump administration's drug pricing pressure campaign, which began in 2025, has evolved to a new level. President Trump signed an executive order in 2025 demanding MFN pricing and sent letters to 17 of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies warning of import tariffs if they failed to lower US drug prices. Pfizer was the first to reach an agreement in September 2025, followed by AstraZeneca and EMD Serono. In November of the same year, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk agreed to significantly cut prices on their popular obesity and diabetes treatments, and in December, nine major pharmaceutical companies—including Amgen, BMS, Gilead, GSK, Merck, Novartis, and Sanofi—signed on the same day. Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie joined in January of this year, with Regeneron becoming the latest to sign in April.

She handed the pharmacist the same prescription she had filled for three years, and the price had multiplied overnight without a single phone call from her plan. Here is what Medicare is allowed to change on January 1 and how…
By
Gerelyn Terzo
Published August 31, 2026, 4:30pm ET · 3 min read
The Full Benefits Desk
desk. Editor:
Gerelyn Terzo
.
𝕏

⧉
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Many seniors, like the woman pictured, face challenges with fluctuating prescription drug costs due to annual changes in Medicare formularies. Unexpected increases can cause significant financial stress.
© wagnerokasaki / E+ via Getty Images
A 72-year-old walks into her pharmacy on January 5 and hands over the same prescription she has filled every month for three years. The copay was $12 in December. Now the pharmacist is asking for $87.
Her doctor did not change the prescription. She did not change plans. The drug simply moved to a costlier tier when the new plan year began. The warning arrived months earlier, buried in the Medicare mail that is easy to mistake for routine paperwork.
January 1 Can Change the Drug Plan You Thought You Kept
Every January, the drug coverage you had in December can come back looking different. A medication can move to a more expensive tier, pick up a new approval hurdle or disappear from the formulary altogether.
The warning usually arrives months earlier in the
Annual Notice of Change (ANOC)
, the packet Medicare drug plans send each fall outlining what will be different in the coming year. By the time the pharmacist tells you the price changed in January, the plan may already consider you notified.
That is what makes automatic renewal so deceptive. You can keep the same insurance card and the same plan name while the deductible, copays, pharmacy deals and treatment of your prescriptions change underneath you.
An $87 Copay May Not Be the Worst Surprise
A formulary change can show up several ways.
A $12 medication can move to a higher tier. A familiar prescription can suddenly require prior authorization. Step therapy can force the patient to try another drug first. Or the medication can vanish from the formulary altogether.
Medicare does provide a bridge in many of those situations. Part D transition rules can allow a temporary supply of an ongoing medication that the new coverage does not include or now subjects to certain restrictions. That gives the patient and prescriber time to switch drugs or request an exception.
It is a bridge, not a permanent solution.
The 2026 Part D benefit also caps annual out-of-pocket spending on covered drugs at $2,100. But a medication the plan will not cover can create a different problem: money paid entirely outside the Part D benefit generally does not get rescued simply because the beneficiary reached the cap.
The Cheapest Premium Can Still Be the Expensive Plan
That is why comparing Part D premiums alone can be misleading.
A $0 or low-premium plan that places one expensive maintenance drug on an unfavorable tier can cost more over the year than a plan charging a higher monthly premium but treating the prescription more generously.
Pharmacy choice matters too. A drug can cost one amount at a preferred pharmacy and considerably more somewhere else.
Higher-income beneficiaries also pay a separate Part D income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA), which sits on top of the plan’s own costs and does not disappear simply because the member switches plans. IRMAA and other premium traps are among those we mapped in a
free Medicare guide
.
Before Letting the Plan Renew Itself, Make These Three Checks
A few minutes spent on the drug list in the fall can prevent an unpleasant conversation at the pharmacy in January:
Open the ANOC and check every regular medication for tier changes, new coverage rules or removal from the formulary.
During open enrollment, enter each drug, dose and preferred pharmacy into Medicare Plan Finder and compare total expected annual costs, not premiums alone.
If January arrives and a medication is no longer covered, ask the plan immediately about a transition fill and have the prescriber pursue a formulary or coverage-rule exception when medically appropriate.
The prescription in her hand may be exactly the same one she filled in December. What changed was the coverage around it. Catching that move in the fall gives her the most choices.

for any questions or corrections.

NPPA Proposes Making Drugmakers Solely Liable for Overpricing Essential Medicines: Report
Subscribe to Notifications
Written By :
Parthika Patel
Published On 2026-08-31 11:53 GMT   |
Update On 2026-08-31 11:53 GMT
New Delhi:
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has proposed making pharmaceutical manufacturers solely responsible for overpricing of essential medicines, a move that could potentially shield retail chemists, nursing homes and hospitals from prosecution for pricing violations, according to a recent media report in The Economic Times.
Under the existing provisions of Para 26 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 (DPCO 2013), no entity is permitted to sell a formulation to a consumer at a price higher than the prevailing price list or the price printed on the container label. For medicines included in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), revised prices become applicable from the date on which the pricing orders are issued.
However, the implementation of revised prices has remained a concern, particularly in cases where retailers continue to sell their existing stocks at the older, higher prices even after a price reduction has taken effect.
According to the proposal under consideration, the provision that currently allows the NPPA to prosecute dealers, retailers or hospitals could be removed in cases where there is clear evidence that these entities knowingly sold medicines at prices exceeding the revised rates.
If implemented, the proposed change would place sole legal responsibility on drug manufacturers for pricing violations across the distribution chain, including instances where medicines are ultimately sold at an excessive price by retailers or hospitals. This could mean that manufacturers would remain liable for violations occurring at the downstream level, even when the actual overcharging is carried out by an entity beyond the manufacturer's direct control.
Also Read:Delhi Health Dept rejects overpricing allegations in CPA procurements amid probe
The government, however, would continue to retain its authority to recover the amount charged in excess of the permitted price. In addition to recovery of the overcharged amount, a penal interest of 15% would also continue to be imposed.
The proposed move has reportedly drawn opposition from pharmaceutical industry stakeholders, who have termed the approach unilateral, biased and unfair. Senior industry officials have raised concerns that manufacturers could be penalised for the actions of retailers, hospitals and other downstream entities that knowingly continue to sell stocks at prices that were applicable before a price revision.
Industry representatives have argued that if a retailer, hospital or other seller is aware of a reduction in the price of a medicine but deliberately continues to sell existing stock at the earlier, higher rate, responsibility for such an action should not rest entirely with the manufacturer. They contend that manufacturers may have little or no control over the price ultimately charged to consumers after the product has moved through the distribution network.
The proposed changes come against the backdrop of significant enforcement action by the NPPA in relation to drug pricing violations. Through March 2026, the regulator had filed 2,737 cases involving pricing violations. The cumulative penalties imposed in these cases stood at ₹8,447 crore, while the regulator had recovered ₹1,582 crore from manufacturers.
The broader issue of pharmaceutical price regulation has also been examined by a parliamentary committee. A recent parliamentary committee report called for a shift away from the existing market-based pricing mechanism, which is based on average retailer margins, towards a hybrid cost- and value-based pricing model. The proposed approach seeks to ensure fair pricing for novel medical interventions while also supporting the sustainability of the pharmaceutical industry.
Economic Times
reports that the proposed NPPA changes could significantly alter the allocation of responsibility for medicine pricing violations, particularly in cases involving revised prices and existing stocks held by retailers, hospitals and other downstream sellers.
The recommendations come amid the continuing debate over how India can ensure access to affordable essential medicines while also maintaining a pricing framework that remains commercially sustainable for pharmaceutical manufacturers and supports the availability of innovative treatments.

TOKYO and CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Aug. 31, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Eisai Co., Ltd. and Biogen Inc. (Nasdaq: BIIB), announced today that Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA-AMC) has issued a final recommendation supporting public reimbursement of LEQEMBI
®
(lecanemab) for eligible patients in Canada living with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease (early AD).
The final recommendation follows a reconsideration by CDA-AMC and is an important step toward access to LEQEMBI. Next steps include negotiations through the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance (pCPA), followed by individual reimbursement decisions by public drug plans in Canada’s provinces and territories.
More than 770,000 people in Canada were estimated to be living with dementia in 2025, and the number of people living with dementia in Canada is projected to increase to 1.7 million by 2050.¹
Eisai serves as the lead for lecanemab’s development and regulatory submissions globally, with Eisai and Biogen co-commercializing and co-promoting the product and Eisai having final decision-making authority.

About lecanemab (generic name, brand name: LEQEMBI
®
)
Lecanemab is the result of a strategic research alliance between Eisai and BioArctic. It is a humanized immunoglobulin gamma (IgG1) monoclonal antibody directed against aggregated soluble (protofibril) and insoluble forms of amyloid-beta (Aβ).
Lecanemab has been approved in 53 countries and regions including Japan, the U.S., China, Europe, South Korea, Taiwan, and Saudi Arabia, and is under regulatory review in 6 countries. Following the initial phase with treatment every two weeks for 18 months, intravenous (IV) maintenance dosing with treatment every four weeks is approved in 8 countries including the U.S., China, the UK, and others, and applications have been filed in 12 countries and regions. The U.S. FDA approved Eisai’s Biologics License Application (BLA) for subcutaneous maintenance dosing with LEQEMBI IQLIK in August 2025. For subcutaneous initiation treatment (500 mg), approval was obtained in the United States in July 2026, and applications are under review in four countries, including Japan and China. In China, the application has been granted Priority Review designation. Since December 2025, lecanemab (IV) has been included in the “Commercial Insurance Innovative Drug List,” recently introduced by the National Healthcare Security Administration (NHSA) of China.
Since July 2020 the Phase 3 clinical study (AHEAD 3-45) for individuals with preclinical AD, meaning they are clinically normal and have intermediate or elevated levels of amyloid in their brains, is ongoing. AHEAD 3-45 is conducted as a public-private partnership between the Alzheimer's Clinical Trial Consortium that provides the infrastructure for academic clinical trials in AD and related dementias in the U.S, funded by the National Institute on Aging, part of the National Institutes of Health, Eisai and Biogen. Since January 2022, the Tau NexGen clinical study for Dominantly Inherited AD (DIAD), that is conducted by Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network Trials Unit (DIAN-TU), led by Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, is ongoing and includes lecanemab as the backbone anti-amyloid therapy.
About Protofibrils
Protofibrils are thought to be the most toxic Aβ species that contribute to brain damage in AD and play a major role in the cognitive decline of this progressive and devastating disease. Protofibrils can cause neuronal and synaptic damage in the brain, which can subsequently adversely affect cognitive function through multiple mechanisms.
2
The mechanism by which this occurs has been reported not only by increasing the formation of insoluble Aβ plaques, but also by directly damaging signaling between neurons and other cells. It is believed that reducing protofibrils may reduce neuronal damage and cognitive impairment, potentially preventing the progression of AD.
3
About the Collaboration between Eisai and Biogen for AD
Eisai and Biogen have been collaborating on the joint development and commercialization of AD treatments since 2014. Eisai serves as the lead of lecanemab development and regulatory submissions globally with both companies co-commercializing and co-promoting the product and Eisai having final decision-making authority.
About the Collaboration between Eisai and BioArctic for AD
Since 2005, Eisai and BioArctic have had a long-term collaboration regarding the development and commercialization of AD treatments. Eisai obtained the global rights to study, develop, manufacture and market lecanemab for the treatment of AD pursuant to an agreement with BioArctic in December 2007. The development and commercialization agreement on the antibody lecanemab back-up was signed in May 2015.
About Eisai Co., Ltd.
Eisai's Corporate Concept is "to give first thought to patients and people in the daily living domain, and to increase the benefits that health care provides." Under this Concept (also known as

With a global network of R&D facilities, manufacturing sites and marketing subsidiaries, we strive to create and deliver innovative products to target diseases with high unmet medical needs, with a particular focus in our strategic areas of Neurology and Oncology.
In addition, we demonstrate our commitment to the elimination of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), which is a target (3.3) of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), by working on various activities together with global partners.

Pharma Policy.content:
Lisa Henderson
,
VP, Editorial
,
Informa Life Sciences
August 31, 2026
2 Min Read
Depositphotos | @ Loran4a
Nearly a quarter of patients attempting to fill prescriptions for Medicare-negotiated drugs faced initial rejections in the first quarter of 2026, matching rates from the previous year and raising questions about whether landmark drug pricing reforms are delivering meaningful benefits to patients.
According to
IQVIA
, these findings come from data three months after maximum fair prices (MFPs) took effect on January 1, 2026, and included the first 10 drugs selected under the Medicare drug price negotiation program. While the Inflation Reduction Act—on which the MFP is predicated—requires Medicare Part D plans to cover these medications on their formularies, the data reveals that coverage does not guarantee access.
According to the author, Rahel Ehrenberg, principal, US Market Access Strategy Consulting at IQVIA,
the 24% overall initial prescription rejection rate masks large differences across therapeutic categories. Patients seeking immunology and oncology medications faced rejection rates of 59% and 67%, respectively—almost double (or triple) the 30% and 21% rates for diabetes and cardiovascular drugs.
Related:
Pharma's 340B problem: 35 years of policy drift
The 10 drugs analyzed—including blood thinners Eliquis and Xarelto, diabetes medications Januvia and Jardiance, and immunology treatment Stelara—represent some of Medicare’s highest-expenditure medications and were the first subject to price negotiations.
While some patients successfully navigated the rejection process, 5% remained unable to access their prescribed medications 30 days after their initial attempt. This also includes 22% of immunology claims and 16% of oncology claims remained rejected after a month, compared to 6% for diabetes and 4% for cardiovascular medications.
With insurers continuing to impose prior authorizations, step therapies, and other restrictions despite the coverage mandate, the report stated that “price negotiation policies should be evaluated not only for government savings but also for their direct effects on patient access and affordability.” As such, the need for continued monitoring of patient access metrics, including both rejection rates and out-of-pocket costs at the point of sale, is suggested by Ehrenberg.

Pharma Policy.content:
By
Gabe Whisnant
and
Dan Gooding
0
Share
Newsweek is a Trust Project member

President
Donald Trump
on Monday announced agreements with nine additional drug manufacturers as part of his administration's effort to lower prescription drug costs.
The agreements are part of the administration's "Most Favored Nation" (MFN) drug pricing initiative, which seeks to align U.S. prescription drug prices with the lowest prices paid in other developed countries. The White House said the new deals bring the total number of participating drugmakers to 26 and cover approximately 89 percent of the branded pharmaceutical market.
Trump has made medication costs a core part of his health care policy during his second term, with Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. telling reporters in the Oval Office that the president said their jobs depended on achieving his goal of lower costs for consumers.
Read More
on
U.S.
"For decades, Americans paid the highest drug prices anywhere in the world, by far," Trump said. "It wasn't even close. We were ripped off by the pharmaceutical companies, we were ripped off, more than anything, by other countries in the world."
Newsweek
reached out to HHS for further comment on Monday afternoon.
Which Manufacturers Are Included?
The companies include Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals and UCB.
As part of the deals, several companies committed to maintain supply reserves and lower costs for specific medicines, including UCB's seizure treatment levetiracetam, Astellas' transplant drug tacrolimus, Sun Pharma's antibiotics clindamycin and doxycycline, and Teva's metronidazole and blood pressure medication amlodipine.
The agreements also cover treatments for conditions including hemophilia, Parkinson's disease, glaucoma, macular degeneration and certain cancers.
According to the White House, the manufacturers have agreed to provide MFN pricing to state Medicaid programs and to ensure future innovative medicines are offered to Americans at prices comparable to those available in other developed nations. The administration said the agreements could generate billions of dollars in savings for Medicaid and patients.
“Teva appreciates the opportunity to work with President Trump and his Administration to expand access and affordability for patients today while enabling continued investment in medicines patients need tomorrow,” Chris Fox, president of Teva USA, said in a press release.
“Teva built its business around delivering affordable medicines to Americans, and we share the Administration’s commitment to improve access to more affordable medicines while investing in scientific innovation and domestic manufacturing capabilities in the U.S.”
...
Which Drugs Are Getting Price Reductions?
The White House did not initially provide a complete list of affected medicines. Instead, it said the agreements cover products used to treat a range of costly and chronic conditions, including:
Hemophilia
Parkinson's disease
Macular degeneration
Glaucoma
Liver diseases
Skin conditions
Various forms of cancer
Related Story
Medicare Update: Court Rules on Seniors’ Drug Price Negotiations
How Trump Moves Differ From Previous Efforts
The Trump administration's approach differs from the Medicare drug-price negotiation program established under former President Joe Biden's Inflation Reduction Act.
The IRA authorizes Medicare to negotiate prices for selected high-cost medications used by seniors. Trump's MFN initiative instead seeks voluntary agreements with manufacturers and ties pricing to rates paid in foreign countries, with a particular focus on Medicaid programs and direct-to-patient sales.
Administration officials have argued that the strategy addresses what they describe as "global freeloading" by foreign governments that benefit from lower drug prices while pharmaceutical companies recover costs through higher U.S. prices. Pharmaceutical companies and some industry groups have previously warned that aggressive pricing restrictions could reduce revenues used for research and development.
What Is MFN Pricing?
Monday's announcement is the latest step in an effort underway since 2025, when Trump revived a version of the "Most Favored Nation" pricing concept through executive action. The policy is based on the argument that Americans pay substantially more for brand-name medications than patients in other wealthy countries because pharmaceutical companies accept lower prices overseas while charging more in the United States.
In July 2025, Trump sent letters to 17 major drug manufacturers demanding that they lower U.S. prices to match those available in comparable developed nations or face potential government action. The administration also called on manufacturers to provide MFN pricing to Medicaid programs and expand direct-to-consumer sales channels.
Those efforts led to a series of agreements throughout late 2025 and 2026 involving some of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, including Pfizer, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Amgen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Gilead Sciences, Merck and Novartis.
What Is TrumpRX?
The White House has also promoted the TrumpRx platform, which allows participating manufacturers to sell certain medicines directly to patients at reduced prices. The administration has argued that bypassing intermediaries such as pharmacy benefit managers can help lower out-of-pocket costs.
Manufacturing Commitments
Alongside the pricing agreements, the White House announced that the nine companies collectively committed to invest at least $19.6 billion in U.S. manufacturing.
Officials said several manufacturers will also contribute drug ingredients to the Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Reserve to strengthen domestic pharmaceutical supply chains and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers during emergencies.
“Working with the U.S. Government reflects our commitment to support access to medicines for people who need them, while continuing to advance the science and innovation that can make a meaningful difference for people living with severe diseases," UCB’s CEO Jean-Christophe Tellier said in a press release. "These priorities, and our contribution to the United States through research, manufacturing, and highly skilled jobs, are essential to our long-term commitment to patients.”

Pharma Policy.content:
Source: Wikipedia/
Mathieu Landretti
,
CC BY-SA 4.0
, via Wikimedia Commons
The White House announced Monday that nine more pharmaceutical manufacturers — including Teva Pharmaceuticals, Sun Pharma, Alcon, and Astellas Pharma — have signed onto President Trump's voluntary Most-Favored-Nation drug pricing framework, pushing the total number of participating companies to 26 and covering an estimated 89% of the U.S. branded drug market.
The expansion builds on a program Trump revived through
an executive order signed in May 2025
, which directed federal health agencies to set drug price targets for Medicare and Medicaid based on prices paid in other wealthy nations. As reported by
WBFF
, the administration had already lined up deals with companies including Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and Pfizer before Monday's additions, and per Bloomberg drugmakers are expected to align prices paid by U.S. states with the costs those same companies charge foreign governments.
The reference basket driving those target prices covers eight high-income countries — Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Switzerland and the United Kingdom — according to
Fierce Pharma
. The gap those benchmarks are meant to close is substantial: a RAND Corporation study using 2022 data found U.S. manufacturer gross prices for brand-name originator drugs averaged 422% of prices across 33 comparison nations, even though American generic drug prices ran 33% below foreign averages.
How the Deals Actually Work
Under the agreements, companies are expected to offer discounts on drugs sold to state Medicaid programs and to list medications on TrumpRx, a presidential portal where Americans can buy prescriptions at reduced cash prices, per WBFF's reporting. Some companies in the MFN deals are also spending billions of dollars to bring manufacturing back to the United States, though the exact impact on patients' out-of-pocket costs remains unclear.
There's a wrinkle that complicates the White House's savings pitch: Medicaid already receives generous discounts from drugmakers under existing federal law, independent of any new voluntary deal. Federal statute requires brand-name manufacturers to provide state Medicaid programs a basic rebate of at least 23.1% of the Average Manufacturer Price, or the difference between that price and the drug's best price, whichever is greater, according to
KFF
. That statutory floor, in place since the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990, leaves open exactly how much additional savings the new Medicaid rebate terms actually deliver.
A Pattern of Price Hikes Despite the Deals
Consumer advocates have raised a more pointed concern: the voluntary structure of MFN agreements does not legally cap the list prices companies charge on existing drugs. A Public Citizen analysis published earlier this month found that all 16 pharmaceutical companies that signed initial MFN deals with the administration went on to raise list prices on 272 drugs in early 2026. Hoodline
previously reported
that a Senate report led by Sen. Bernie Sanders reached a similar conclusion, showing drugmakers hiked list prices on hundreds of medicines after entering the pricing agreements.
Biotech companies, meanwhile, would be exempt from Medicare pilot programs mandating similar discounts, per Bloomberg. The administration is not the first to try an MFN-style approach: during Trump's first term, CMS issued an interim final rule for Medicare Part B in November 2020, only to see federal district courts block it with nationwide preliminary injunctions after pharmaceutical trade groups sued over Administrative Procedure Act violations. CMS formally rescinded that rule in December 2021.
Voluntary Deals Versus Mandatory Negotiation
The voluntary MFN push stands in contrast to a legally binding mechanism already in effect: the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 mandated Medicare drug price negotiations, and the first set of lower negotiated prices for 10 high-expenditure Part D medications — including blockbusters like Eliquis and Jardiance — took effect on January 1 of this year, according to KFF. Unlike the MFN agreements, that statutory negotiation process carries the force of tax penalties for noncompliance.
Some drugmakers appear to be recalibrating their global pricing strategies in anticipation of continued MFN pressure. AstraZeneca executives disclosed on a Q2 2026 investor call that the company restructured its global launch pricing for new medicines specifically to adapt to the reference-pricing push,
Hoodline reported
at the time. The administration has also paired the pricing push with trade pressure: Trump announced a phased tariff schedule on imported generic drugs in July, keeping duties at zero through August 1 before ramping to 100% in 2028 and 200% in 2029, a policy Hoodline covered as part of its push to get drugmakers to build manufacturing plants domestically.
Trump is expected to sign a deal with nearly a dozen drugmakers to voluntarily sell medications for less, per an MS NOW report cited by WBFF, as part of a broader White House effort to spotlight healthcare affordability ahead of the midterms. The administration has previously announced Most-Favored-Nation drug pricing deals with 17 pharmaceutical companies, and Monday's addition of nine more manufacturers marks the latest expansion of a policy the White House continues to promote as a centerpiece of its economic agenda.

Pharma Policy.content:
Ministry of Health and Welfare Registers 'Fintepla Solution' in Just 126 Days
New Coverage for 'Polivy', Expanded Application for 'Blincyto'
Support for Stable Supply of Withdrawal-Prevention Medicines Also Strengthened
With the expansion of health insurance coverage for treatments targeting serious and rare diseases, the financial burden of high treatment costs on patients is set to decrease. In particular, a Dravet syndrome therapy was registered as a reimbursable drug through a pilot project that conducted approval, reimbursement review, and price negotiation simultaneously, allowing it to be listed for health insurance at nearly twice the speed compared to the previous process.
View original image
Starting September 1, the Ministry of Health and Welfare announced it will expand pharmaceutical reimbursement under the health insurance program to alleviate the treatment cost burden on patients with rare and intractable diseases and those with serious cancers. The Ministry also stated it would support the stable supply of essential medicines where supply disruptions are of concern.
With this expansion, health insurance will now cover Fintepla Oral Solution, a treatment for Dravet syndrome, a rare and intractable form of epilepsy. Dravet syndrome is a disease that manifests within a child's first year and leads to severe seizures and developmental delays. The estimated number of patients in Korea is about 150. Due to frequent, severe seizures, treatment is complex and the costs are considerable.
Thanks to insurance coverage for Fintepla Oral Solution, the annual medical expense per patient, which was around 100 million won, is expected to be reduced to about 10 million won.
Notably, Fintepla Oral Solution was selected for the 'Simultaneous Approval-Evaluation-Negotiation Pilot Project' aimed at accelerating insurance reimbursement of drugs for critical illnesses. The product was approved by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety, with the reimbursement review by the Health Insurance Review & Assessment Service and price negotiations with the National Health Insurance Service conducted simultaneously. As a result, insurance listing was completed in 126 days—significantly faster than the usual 240-day process.
For initial treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignant blood cancer marked by abnormal B-cell proliferation, the newly developed drug Polivy Injection is now reimbursable. While initial treatment options have until now been limited, this reimbursement expansion is expected to provide patients with new therapeutic choices.
The scope of health insurance coverage for Blincyto Injection, a pediatric leukemia medication, will also be broadened. Previously, reimbursement for patients with precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia was only available if the disease relapsed or did not respond to established treatments. Now, patients will be eligible for reimbursement even in the early stage to remove minimal residual disease following first-line chemotherapy, immediately after cancer cells have been eradicated. As this disease shows a higher incidence in children under five, the Ministry of Health and Welfare expects this move will help reduce the risk of early relapse and raise the chances of complete cure.
Efforts to support the stable supply of essential medicines will also be reinforced. The Ministry has newly designated JW Protamine 6% Injection—a drug vital for blood pressure regulation and circulatory stability in newborns and premature infants—as an 'exit prevention medication' where low profitability raises risks of discontinued production or import, and is implementing a cost compensation scheme. Tuberculin PPD AJV, an essential tuberculosis diagnostic reagent for which supply disruptions were expected due to increased import prices, will have those higher unit costs quickly reflected in this year's pricing to preempt any supply instability.

Pharma Policy.url_match_title: EXCLUSIVE: Biden’s IRA price control architects under scrutiny as Republicans hammer health care affordability challenges - Washington Reporter
Pharma Policy.content:
As Republicans make health care affordability a midterm issue, new scrutiny is falling on a senior Biden administration official who helped build a Medicare overhaul that was sold as a major money saver, but is now projected to increase federal deficits.
Kristi Martin, the former chief of staff at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), played a key role implementing the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and its Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program. Before joining the Biden administration, Martin worked for organizations that had pushed aggressive government intervention in prescription drug pricing, and
reportedly
had a reputation for heavily favoring hospital and insurance interests.
The scrutiny comes after a July letter from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) delivered a significant blow to the fiscal case Democrats made for the IRA.
When Democrats passed the law in 2022, the CBO projected that three major Medicare drug provisions — drug-price negotiations, inflation rebates and a redesign of Medicare Part D — would collectively reduce federal deficits by $129 billion through 2031.
Four years later, the CBO says that calculation has flipped.
“Evidence now indicates that the spending reductions attributable to drug price negotiation and inflation rebates have been smaller than CBO originally estimated,” the agency reported. Costs from the Part D redesign, meanwhile, have been “significantly larger.”
The CBO now projects the three provisions will increase federal deficits through 2031.
The reversal could give Republicans ammunition as they argue that government bureaucracy, insurers, and other middlemen are swallowing an increasing share of Americans’ health care dollars.
It also raises questions about the officials who designed the Biden program.
Martin previously served as vice president for health care at Arnold Ventures, where she led the organization’s prescription drug pricing portfolio. She also worked as managing director of the health practice at Waxman Strategies, founded by former Rep. Henry Waxman (D., Calif.), and served as a senior adviser in the Obama administration’s Office of Health Reform. Federal Election Commission (FEC) records show Martin contributed to Democratic candidates, including Joe Biden and Elizabeth Warren.
While at CMS, Martin helped oversee implementation of the IRA’s drug provisions and the construction of the bureaucracy responsible for administering them.
The program’s fiscal performance has fallen short of initial expectations.
The CBO originally assumed the first round of negotiations would produce average net price reductions of approximately 50 percent. Actual reductions were roughly 22 percent relative to 2023 net prices, prompting the agency to increase projected Medicare spending.
The larger problem has been Part D.
The CBO found that insurers’ 2026 bids reflected an approximately 35 percent increase in annual costs per enrollee, compared with the roughly 5 percent increase the agency had expected. The CBO concluded that the IRA’s Part D redesign was the “leading driver” of the unexpectedly high bids.
That record is now generating another question among some Republicans and health care policy analysts, several of whom raised questions to the
Washington Reporter
. At the forefront of the unanswered questions is why is CMS under President Donald Trump continuing a system created under Biden? While Martin left CMS before President Trump took office, the system she designed and the team she worked with to enact it have remained completely intact.
Republican health policy sources who spoke with the
Reporter
questioned why an administration that has aggressively dismantled Biden policies elsewhere is maintaining the basic framework Martin helped establish, even as we see it fail on such a massive scale.
“It’s strange to see officials within President Trump’s CMS effectively maintaining a Biden program, designed by Biden officials, and still being run by many of the same leftover Biden bureaucrats,” one Republican source familiar with the issue told the
Reporter
.
The criticism comes as officials within President Trump’s CMS are doing more than simply finishing negotiations inherited from Biden. In June, CMS proposed establishing a “permanent framework” for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program beginning with drugs whose negotiated prices take effect in 2029. CMS Administrator, Dr. Mehmet Oz, said the administration was moving from annual updates to a “permanent, predictable framework.”
CMS followed that action in July with additional guidance for implementing negotiated prices in 2028.
The Trump administration has also expanded the program into its third negotiation cycle, selecting 15 additional drugs, including Medicare Part B drugs for the first time, for negotiations occurring this year.
Personnel continuity is also drawing attention.Daniel Heider was named Director of CMS in June 2023 under the Biden administration, after donating to the Biden presidential campaign in 2020; he also donated to as well as contributions to 2020 Democratic Senate candidates including Sara Gideon, Theresa Greenfield, Steve Bullock, and Barbara Bollier, all of whom were defeated by Republicans
Another Biden connection is Lara Strawbridge, who was named Acting Director of the Medicare Drug Rebate and Negotiations Group at the Center For Medicare & Medicaid Services under the Biden administration; she has previous ties to nonprofits connected to the Arabella Advisors network, and she also
contributed
to Kamala Harris’s failed presidential campaign.
Heider and Strawbridge were both reportedly in the room when the program in question was developed, sources told the
Reporter
.
Another health care  source said the continued presence of officials involved in Biden-era implementation with such obvious partisan leanings makes the administration’s embrace of the program particularly difficult to reconcile with Republican attacks on the IRA.
“If Republicans are going to run on cleaning up the health care mess Biden left behind, they can’t keep Biden’s system on autopilot,” the source said. “You can’t argue that these policies failed seniors and taxpayers and then leave the same structure and the same people in charge of carrying them out.”

Pharma Policy.content:
The
Trump administration
announced nine new drug price reduction deals with midsize pharmaceutical companies in an effort to continue lowering prescription drug costs ahead of the November midterm elections.
President Donald Trump said Monday during an Oval Office event that the new deals are “as big as it gets medically.”
Recommended Stories

Fact check: Trump claims no autism cases among unvaccinated Amish children
Trump announces nine new most-favored-nation deals to lower prescription prices
“It’s the largest drug discount, the largest price reductions in the history of medicine,” Trump said. “I would say that’s pretty big.”
Advertisement
The
nine companies
are Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals, and UCB.
They joined 17 larger drugmakers in signing most-favored-nation drug deals with the Trump administration, agreeing to reduce the prices at which their drugs are sold in the United States to the same level as the lowest on the market in other developed countries.
Trump said the nine new companies have agreed to “offer all of their drugs to state Medicaid programs at most-favored-nation prices” and offer all new medications to U.S. consumers “at the lowest cost anywhere in the world.”
Advertisement
FACT SHEET
President Donald J. Trump Announces Deal with Nine Additional Pharmaceutical Manufacturers to Lower Drug Prices for Americans
President Trump announced agreements with nine additional pharmaceutical manufacturers to lower prescription drug prices for Americans,…
— whitehouse.gov News (@whgovnews)
August 31, 2026
Pharmaceutical prices fell by
0.8% in July and are down 3.1% from last year
, the steepest annual decline in more than 60 years, according to the most recent Consumer Price Index report.
Chris Klomp
, senior adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and chief negotiator of the MFN deals, said the drop in drug prices is a result of the drug pricing deals as well as TrumpRx, the aggregator website.
“These are real impacts for everyday Americans in their pockets,” Klomp said. “It’s affordability. It’s the president fighting for affordability. It’s the president honoring the promise to fight for affordability and doing it in one of the most conspicuous places possible, which is at the pharmacy counter.”
Advertisement
Trump also said the companies are committing “billions of dollars to research and development in the United States.”
The president credited the threat of tariffs on foreign imported drugs and what he called his “America First” trade policy for getting pharmaceutical companies to invest in drug production in the U.S.
He also said the pharmaceutical companies that signed on to Monday’s deal are committing to contribute a combined 290 metric tons of active pharmaceutical ingredients to the U.S. strategic reserve.
Advertisement
“By stockpiling such materials in vast quantities, we can ensure Americans are never left without them in the event of an emergency,” Trump said.
Dr.
Heidi Overton
, a White House health policy adviser and Trump’s nominee for Food and Drug Administration commissioner, said the administration’s goal ought to be maintaining dominance in cutting-edge research in addition to onshoring drug manufacturing.
“We want every part of clinical research, clinical trials done here in America to both protect our national security and to make it more affordable,” Overton said. “And under your leadership, we can do both.”
Advertisement
Administration officials have been pressuring Congress to codify MFN drug deals into law so that the reductions in prices cannot be undone by another administration.
AMERICANS CARE MORE ABOUT HEALTHCARE AFFORDABILITY THAN GAS OR GROCERIES
Trump said he does not imagine that the next president “would be brave enough” to reverse his policies and inevitably raise prescription prices.
“But it’s still good to have it codified, have it approved by Congress,” Trump said.

African Traditional Medicine Key to Universal Health Coverage – WHO
Africa on Monday marked the 24th African Traditional Medicine Day, with experts urging governments to invest more in research, regulation and innovation to unlock traditional medicine’s potential for universal health coverage.
The World Health Organisation (WHO), in a post on its official X account on Monday, said the Aug. 31 observance focused on strengthening traditional medicine as a credible contributor to Africa’s healthcare systems.
According to WHO, the theme, “Reflection on research and development efforts of traditional medicine towards achieving universal health coverage in the African Region,” underscores the need to transform knowledge into solutions.
The organisation said the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and WHO Regional Office for Africa convened stakeholders to examine how evidence, innovation and community trust could move traditional medicine into practice.
WHO said this year’s observance highlighted research and development efforts aimed at making traditional medicine more accessible, safer and evidence-based, while supporting universal health coverage across African countries.
“Participants said traditional medicine could strengthen primary healthcare when supported by scientific evidence, effective regulation, innovation and sustained investment,” WHO said, emphasising the sector’s growing healthcare relevance.
“African Traditional Medicine Day commemorates a landmark WHO resolution adopted during the organisation’s 50th Regional Committee meeting in Ouagadougou in 2000.
“Traditional medicine remains an important source of healthcare, particularly in rural communities where practitioners often serve as the first point of contact,” the organisation said.
According to WHO, experts noted that traditional health practitioners possess deep community relationships and cultural legitimacy that can complement conventional healthcare systems and improve access to quality services.
The organisation said Mr Temitayo Erogbogbo, Global Advocacy Director at Merck Sharp and Dohme for Mothers, emphasised that trust remained a critical asset within traditional healthcare networks.
According to WHO, Erogbogbo said traditional birth attendants, community healers and other practitioners maintain longstanding relationships that can support better health outcomes when appropriately integrated into healthcare delivery.
WHO said Prof. Martins Emeje, Director-General of the Nigeria Natural Medicine Development Agency, participated in the discussion, bringing perspectives on advancing traditional medicine through scientific validation and innovation.
The organisation said that Emeje also serves as Co-Chair of the WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group for Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine, supporting global policy and research efforts.
According to WHO, participants emphasised that traditional medicine should not be viewed as a relic of the past but as a living knowledge system requiring evidence and innovation.
The experts said that Africa possessed vast traditional health knowledge and biodiversity resources capable of driving healthcare development, pharmaceutical innovation and economic opportunities across the continent.
However, WHO said participants emphasised that unlocking the potential required stronger collaboration among researchers, policymakers, entrepreneurs, communities and traditional health practitioners working towards shared healthcare goals.
The organisation said stakeholders also called for greater domestic investment in research and development to scientifically investigate, validate and improve traditional medicines for broader healthcare applications.
According to WHO, participants highlighted the urgent need to document traditional medical knowledge to prevent valuable information from disappearing and ensure its preservation for future generations.
The organisation warned that undocumented knowledge risked being permanently lost, making systematic preservation, scientific study and knowledge transfer essential for sustainable healthcare innovation and development efforts.
“The discussion aligned with WHO’s Global Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034, which prioritises research, regulation, integration and collaboration.
“The strategy seeks to promote safe, effective and evidence-based traditional medicine while strengthening people-centred health systems,” WHO said, outlining its vision for healthcare transformation through integration.
“Traditional medicine is already used by millions worldwide and can support prevention, self-care and primary healthcare alongside biomedical services,” the organisation said during the discussion.
According to WHO, experts expressed optimism that innovation, digital tools and growing youth interest could create fresh opportunities for traditional medicine research, entrepreneurship and healthcare advancement.
“They envisioned stronger collaboration between traditional medicine and biomedicine, with both approaches contributing complementary strengths to healthier communities.
“Countries including Cameroon, Madagascar, Mozambique, South Africa and Zimbabwe are commemorating the day through national and regional activities,” the organisation said.
WHO said speakers ultimately called for sustained investment in evidence generation, empowerment of traditional health practitioners and responsible use of Africa’s biodiversity to expand quality healthcare access #African Traditional Medicine Key to Universal Health Coverage – WHO#

Pharma Associations.url_match_title: South Korea’s K-Fold moves beyond the lab into drug discovery as industry group launches hands-on training - The Korea Post
Pharma Associations.content:
South Korea’s home-grown bio-artificial intelligence model K-Fold, developed as a challenger to Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold3, is moving beyond the research and development stage and into the country’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology research sector. Rather than stopping at the development of an independent AI model capable of predicting protein structures and their interactions with potential drug compounds, researchers are now being given hands-on training to use the technology directly in the search for new drug candidates.
The AI Institute for Drug Development at the Korea Pharmaceutical and Bio-Pharma Manufacturers Association (KPBMA) said on 31 August that it would hold a special seminar, “Keeping Up with AI Drug Discovery: An Introduction to K-Fold”, at the association’s headquarters in Seoul’s Seocho district on 1 September. The seminar is intended to explain the development background and operating principles of K-Fold, a next-generation bio-AI model recently unveiled by KAIST, while giving researchers an opportunity to experience how it can be applied in real-world drug discovery.
Poster for the K-Fold introductory session (Source: Korea Pharmaceutical and Bio-Pharma Manufacturers Association)
K-Fold was developed by “Team KAIST”, led by Woo Youn Kim, a professor in KAIST’s Department of Chemistry who previously headed KPBMA’s AI Drug Discovery Support Center. Developed under the Ministry of Science and ICT’s AI Specialized Foundation Model Project, the home-grown bio-AI model can predict not only the three-dimensional structure of proteins but also the structures of complexes formed when proteins interact with drug candidates, other proteins, DNA and RNA.
The key questions are accuracy and speed. In a government project stage evaluation in March, K-Fold’s accuracy in predicting molecular complex structures was assessed as approaching that of Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold3. KAIST said an internal evaluation carried out by the research team in August also found that the model outperformed existing global models in some drug-target areas, including G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), kinases and targeted protein degradation (TPD).
Speed is attracting particular attention among researchers. Conventional AI systems for protein structure prediction can require substantial computing resources for preliminary calculations that involve searching and comparing vast amounts of sequence data from similar proteins. K-Fold reduces its reliance on this process, increasing structure-prediction speeds by up to 25 times compared with existing models. In practical terms, this could allow researchers to examine more drug candidates within the same period and more quickly narrow the pool of compounds to be taken forward for experimental testing.
Behind the technological race is a broader shift in the way new drugs are developed. AI-based protein structure prediction has moved beyond being merely a research aid and is increasingly becoming a core technology in drug design. Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold3 expanded the scope of structural prediction beyond proteins to interactions involving a range of biomolecules, including nucleic acids and small molecules, within a single model. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, who developed AlphaFold2, were jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on protein structure prediction.
The competition surrounding K-Fold therefore goes beyond simply securing a “Korean AlphaFold”. The next challenge is to establish a domestic bio-AI capability that researchers can use independently rather than relying on overseas platforms, and to determine how quickly that technology can be incorporated into pharmaceutical companies’ drug-candidate discovery processes. KAIST has described K-Fold as laying the foundations for “sovereign AI” in biotechnology, while KPBMA and the Korea Biotechnology Industry Organization, or KoreaBIO, are leading efforts to expand its use across industry.
That is also why the seminar places greater emphasis on using the technology than simply explaining it. The session will be led by Sangyeon Hwang, head of the advanced research team at HITS. It will begin with an explanation of the AI Specialized Foundation Model Project and the purpose of the K-Fold training, before covering the model’s development, operating principles, predictive performance and future development. Participants will then use K-Fold directly through HyperLab, a web-based AI research platform. HITS, a KAIST faculty-founded company, has integrated K-Fold into HyperLab so that researchers can use the model without having to build and operate a complex AI environment of their own.
Efforts to expand the technology across industry are already gathering pace. According to KAIST, 85 people took part in an online K-Fold training session organised by KoreaBIO on 27 August, while 118 registered for KPBMA’s hybrid online and in-person session on 1 September. The focus is therefore beginning to move beyond competition over model performance towards building a user base that allows pharmaceutical and biotechnology researchers to incorporate AI directly into drug-design work.
However, accurate structural prediction by AI does not in itself guarantee successful drug development. Even if AI can rapidly narrow down promising binding structures and candidate compounds, their efficacy and toxicity must still be validated through experiments, followed by separate preclinical and clinical stages. Industrial competitiveness will therefore depend not only on benchmark performance but also on how easily researchers can use the model repeatedly, how effectively it can be linked with experimental data, and how much time and money it can actually save in identifying potential drug candidates. As increasingly sophisticated structure-prediction technologies emerge worldwide, K-Fold now faces the test of whether it can turn research achievements into measurable productivity in the laboratory and across industry.
KPBMA President Noh Yeon-hong said technologies such as K-Fold could lower the barriers for researchers seeking to use AI, increase the speed and efficiency of identifying drug candidates and, over the longer term, help strengthen the research and development competitiveness of South Korea’s pharmaceutical and biotechnology industry. Junhee Pyo, director of the AI Institute for Drug Development, said the institute planned to use the seminar as a starting point for further expanding training and collaboration that connects advanced domestic AI technologies with pharmaceutical and biotechnology research.

The AI Institute for Drug Development at the Korea Pharmaceutical and Bio-Pharma Manufacturers Association (KPBMA) said on 31 August that it would hold a special seminar, “Keeping Up with AI Drug Discovery: An Introduction to K-Fold”, at the association’s headquarters in Seoul’s Seocho district on 1 September.

The seminar is intended to explain the development background and operating principles of K-Fold, a next-generation bio-AI model recently unveiled by KAIST, while giving researchers an opportunity to experience how it can be applied in real-world drug discovery.

According to the White House, this deal brings the total number of pharmaceutical companies that have agreed to "most-favored-nation pricing" to 26.

August 31, 2026
MFN Program Grows to 26 Drugmakers as Nine More Commit to $19.6B in US Manufacturing
Author(s)
Nicholas Jacobus
Nine more manufacturers join the MFN program, pairing new Medicaid pricing deals with $19.6B in U.S. manufacturing investment and API reserve donations.
Advertisement
President Donald J. Trump announced nine new Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) agreements with pharmaceutical manufacturers on August 31, bringing the program's total roster to 26 companies. The administration says that group now accounts for 89% of the branded drug market,
1
a milestone with direct implications for how supply chain and market access teams plan pricing, procurement, and Medicaid formulary strategy heading into 2027.
Nine more manufacturers sign on
The newly announced participants are a group of mid-sized manufacturers:
Alcon
Astellas Pharma
BeOne Medicines
BridgeBio
CSL
Kyowa Kirin
Sun Pharma
Teva Pharmaceuticals
UCB
The products affected span a wide swath of costly and chronic therapeutic areas, including hemophilia, Parkinson's disease, macular degeneration, glaucoma, liver disease, dermatologic conditions, and multiple cancers.
1
Under the deals, every state Medicaid program gains access to MFN pricing on these companies' products, which the White House projects will translate into billions of dollars in aggregate savings.
1
A companion White House fact sheet frames the agreements as closing off the ability of other countries to use price controls to benefit from American drug innovation without paying comparable prices.
1
Manufacturing and supply chain commitments take center stage
For supply chain and commercialization leaders, the more consequential piece may be what's attached to the pricing deals rather than the pricing itself. The nine companies have collectively pledged at least $19.6 billion in near-term U.S. manufacturing investment, and several are directing material toward the Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Reserve, a stockpile meant to reduce dependence on foreign API sources and buffer against future supply disruptions.
1
Individual contributions include:
UCB: 163 tons of levetiracetam, an anticonvulsant
Sun Pharma: 71.4 tons of clindamycin and 6.75 tons of doxycycline, both antibiotics
Teva Pharmaceuticals: 45 metric tons of metronidazole (antibiotic/antiprotozoal) and 4.8 tons of amlodipine (antihypertensive)
Astellas: 25 kg of tacrolimus, an immunosuppressant used in transplant care
For sourcing and procurement teams, these donations are worth tracking as an early signal of how manufacturers may reallocate API supply commitments going forward.
What it means for market access
The Medicaid provisions are the piece most relevant to market access and payer-strategy teams, though industry watchers caution the practical effect on patients may be limited. Lindsay Bealor Greenleaf, head of market access policy strategy at ADVI, t
old our sister publication
Pharmaceutical Executiv
e
that Medicaid patients typically already pay only $4 to $8 out of pocket, and that the financial impact of the voluntary deals falls on manufacturers rather than patients. That distinction matters for commercialization planners weighing how MFN participation will affect net pricing and rebate structures rather than front-line patient access.
The road to 26 agreements
The nine deals build on momentum going back to May 2025, when the MFN executive order was signed, followed two months later by letters sent to 17 major manufacturers directing them to bring U.S. list prices in line with the lowest price charged in other developed markets.
2
According to the White House, all 17 of those companies have since signed on.
1
Combined with today's additions, the MFN roster now includes Pfizer, AstraZeneca, EMD Serono, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Amgen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Boehringer Ingelheim, Genentech, Gilead Sciences, GSK, Merck, Novartis, Sanofi, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Regeneron, Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals, and UCB.
1
What remains undone
Even with 26 manufacturers now committed, the administration is pushing Congress to pass the Great Healthcare Plan, broader legislation aimed at lowering drug prices and insurance premiums, increasing accountability for insurers, and expanding price transparency.
3
Unlike the manufacturer-by-manufacturer MFN deals, that agenda depends on legislative action, meaning its outcome, and any further supply chain or market access implications, rests with lawmakers rather than executive negotiation.

Pharma Associations.content:
BRONX, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--
#Alzheimers
--Oligomerix, Inc., a privately held, clinical-stage biotechnology company pioneering the development of novel small molecule therapeutics to address Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and rare neurodegenerative diseases, today announced that Cara Cassino, M.D., has been appointed Interim President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO).
Dr. Cassino has 25 years of clinical drug development and commercialization experience in both large pharma and biotech, with over 25 FDA/EMA drug approvals in a wide range of therapeutic areas. She has held senior leadership roles at Boehringer Ingelheim and Pfizer where she played an important role in the success of the blockbuster respiratory product Spiriva. She later joined Forest Laboratories (now part of Abbvie) as Senior Vice President of Clinical Development at a critical time in the company’s evolution. She subsequently held C-suite positions in biotech, serving as Chief Medical Officer, EVP of Research & Development and Interim Co-CEO at ContraFect Corp, a public biotech, where she led the company‘s successful effort to earn an $86M grant from the Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA). As a highly experienced pharmaceutical industry leader, she brings strategic business experience, a proven track record of portfolio expansion via strategic partnerships and multi-million-dollar M&A deals, as well as a series of successful biotech equity financings totaling over $190M. Dr. Cassino has been a member of the Oligomerix Board of Directors since July 2025.
“We are very pleased to welcome a leader of this caliber, with a depth of clinical development experience. Dr. Cassino joins Oligomerix as Interim President and CEO at a critical time, as the company evolves from a discovery-focused biotech to a clinical-stage drug development organization. Having successfully completed a Phase 1a study of our lead compound (OLX-07010), Dr. Cassino brings tremendous insight, experience and know-how as the company advances OLX-07010 into the next stages of the clinical development,” said Bill Caple, Chairman of Oligomerix.
“I am excited to join Oligomerix as Interim President & CEO and look forward to working with the team to advance OLX-07010 as a novel oral therapeutic with the potential to improve the lives of patients with Alzheimer’s disease and other progressive neurodegenerative diseases,” said Dr. Cassino.
About Oligomerix’s Lead Program
OLX-07010 is a highly differentiated oral, self-administered, once-daily investigational drug that has demonstrated an ability to prevent the accumulation of tau protein in multiple animal models and has completed Phase 1a clinical development, demonstrating a favorable safety profile in healthy volunteers. Given the high unmet medical needs for novel, well tolerated and easily administered new agents to treat AD and other neurodegenerative diseases, Oligomerix looks forward to potentially offering patients with AD a new and effective therapeutic option by advancing OLX-07010 through the next stages of clinical development.
About Oligomerix, Inc.
Oligomerix is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on discovering and developing novel, small-molecule inhibitors of protein self-association and accumulation which underpin AD and rare neurodegenerative diseases such as progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). The company’s headquarters and research laboratories are located at the Ullmann Research Center for Health Sciences within the Albert Einstein College of Medicine.
