Press release
Share
REYKJAVIK, Iceland, August 31, 2026
- Alvotech (NASDAQ: ALVO; ALVO-SDB), a global biotechnology company specializing in the development and manufacture of biosimilar medicines for patients worldwide, today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted for review a Biologics License Application (BLA) for AVT80, a proposed interchangeable biosimilar to Entyvio® (vedolizumab) prefilled syringe and autoinjector for subcutaneous administration.
Under a partnership with Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. (NYSE and TASE: TEVA), Alvotech is responsible for the development and manufacturing of AVT80, while Teva is responsible for commercialization.
“FDA’s acceptance for review of our BLA for AVT80 is another important milestone for our vedolizumab biosimilar program,” said Joseph McClellan, Chief Operating Officer of Alvotech. “Together with our BLA for AVT16, which was accepted for review in May, the program encompasses both intravenous and subcutaneous presentations, including a prefilled syringe and autoinjector.”
Entyvio is a biologic medicine approved for the treatment of adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease.
The BLA submission is supported by a comprehensive data package, including analytical, pharmacokinetic, and immunogenicity data generated to support the demonstration of biosimilarity between AVT80 and the reference product.
AVT80 has been submitted as a proposed interchangeable biosimilar. In the United States, an interchangeable biosimilar may be substituted for the reference product at the pharmacy without the intervention of the prescriber, subject to applicable laws. If approved, AVT80 would add to the range of biosimilar options available to patients and healthcare providers in the United States.
In February 2026, Alvotech announced positive results from a
pivotal pharmacokinetic study
for AVT80. The randomized, double-blind, single-dose, parallel-group, three-arm study compared AVT80 to Entyvio in healthy adult participants and met all its primary endpoints. Based on regulatory advice, the clinical study is considered pivotal to support the demonstration of clinical similarity for both AVT16 and AVT80.
About AVT80 and AVT16
AVT80 is a proposed interchangeable biosimilar candidate to Entyvio (vedolizumab), a humanized monoclonal antibody. It is being developed as a prefilled syringe and autoinjector for subcutaneous administration. AVT80 complements AVT16, Alvotech’s proposed interchangeable biosimilar to Entyvio for intravenous administration for which the FDA
accepted a BLA for review in May 2026
. In the European Union, the European Medicines Agency has validated a Marketing Authorization Application covering both AVT16 (lyophilized vial) and AVT80 (pre-filled syringe and autoinjector).
Together these two candidates form part of Alvotech’s broader pipeline of biosimilar candidates in immunology aimed at expanding access to biologic medicines in major therapeutic areas.
AVT16 and AVT80 are investigational products and have not received regulatory approval in any markets. Biosimilarity and interchangeability have not been established by regulatory authorities and are not claimed.
About Entyvio
Entyvio (vedolizumab) is an integrin receptor antagonist indicated for the treatment of adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease. Vedolizumab targets and binds specifically to the alpha-4-beta-7 integrin, which is involved in the migration of certain white blood cells into gastrointestinal tissue.
Use of trademarks
Entyvio is a registered trademark of Millennium Pharmaceuticals, Inc. The use of this trademark is solely for the purpose of identifying the reference product. Alvotech and Teva do not claim any rights to the trademark.

About Alvotech
Alvotech is a biotechnology company, founded by Robert Wessman, focused solely on the development and manufacture of biosimilar medicines for patients worldwide. Alvotech seeks to be a global leader in the biosimilar space by delivering high-quality, cost-effective products and services, enabled by a fully integrated approach and broad in-house capabilities. Five biosimilars are already approved and marketed in multiple global markets, including biosimilars to Humira® (adalimumab), Stelara® (ustekinumab), Simponi® (golimumab), Eylea® (aflibercept) and Prolia®/Xgeva® (denosumab). The current development pipeline includes disclosed biosimilar candidates aimed at treating autoimmune disorders, eye disorders, and cancer. Alvotech has formed a network of strategic commercial partnerships to provide global reach and leverage local expertise in markets that include the United States, Europe, Japan, China, and other Asian countries and large parts of South America, Africa and the Middle East. Regulatory Agencies.content:
Washington, D.C.--(Newsfile Corp. - August 31, 2026) - The Securities and Exchange Commission and the Food and Drug Administration today announced that they have entered into a
Memorandum of Understanding
(MOU) designed to assist the agencies in carrying out their respective missions of ensuring the integrity of the financial markets and protecting public health.
The MOU establishes a framework for the agencies to enhance cooperation in their regulatory and enforcement responsibilities in order to improve market oversight and compliance. Among other things, the MOU includes information-sharing protocols to facilitate the exchange of information between the SEC and FDA that is relevant to both agencies’ important missions.
“FDA-related disclosures by public companies have a significant impact on our markets,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins. “The FDA is a valuable partner in our efforts to administer and enforce applicable disclosure requirements under the federal securities laws, and I look forward to further strengthening our partnership through the MOU.”
“We are proud to partner with the SEC to enhance transparency across the life sciences sector,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantras J.D. “Streamlining our information-sharing helps protect both the patients who rely on FDA-regulated products and the public trust that drives healthcare innovation.”
The MOU will remain in effect for a period of three years, and it may be extended or modified by the mutual written consent of the agencies.

Alvotech (ALVO)
reports that the U.S. FDA has accepted for review a Biologics License Application (BLA) for AVT80, a proposed interchangeable biosimilar to Entyvio (vedolizumab) in prefilled syringe and autoinjector formats for subcutaneous use. Under its partnership with Teva, Alvotech leads development and manufacturing while Teva handles commercialization.
The BLA is supported by analytical, pharmacokinetic and immunogenicity data, including a randomized, double-blind, single-dose, three-arm pivotal study that met all primary endpoints. AVT80 complements AVT16, Alvotech’s proposed intravenous Entyvio biosimilar, for which the FDA accepted a BLA in May 2026, creating a two-presentation vedolizumab biosimilar program within Alvotech’s broader immunology pipeline. Both AVT16 and AVT80 remain investigational; no regulatory approvals have been granted and biosimilarity or interchangeability is not yet established.

Regulatory Agencies.url_match_title: FDA strips WR blood bank’s licence - Mumbai Mirror
Regulatory Agencies.content:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the licence of a Western Railway-run blood bank at Mumbai Central’s Jagjivan Ram Hospital after uncovering a series of regulatory violations involving blood collection, storage, donor management and statutory compliance.
The action follows a March 2026 inspection that documented 12 deficiencies across critical areas, including donor consent procedures, manpower, blood donation camp records, inventory controls, cold-chain monitoring and quality assurance. After issuing a show-cause notice and conducting a personal hearing, the regulator ordered suspension of the facility’s licence for two days starting from October 15 till 16.
Documents reviewed by Mumbai Mirror show that regulators were concerned by the cumulative nature of the deficiencies, several of which were not documented at the time of inspection and were addressed only after inspectors raised objections. The licensing authority repeatedly rejected explanations submitted by hospital officials, stating that corrective measures taken later could not erase non-compliance that existed during the inspection.
One of the deficiencies involved the use of apheresis donor consent forms that did not conform to prescribed guidelines. Inspectors also found that updated copies of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Indian Pharmacopoeia, essential reference documents for licenced blood banks, were unavailable during the inspection.
The regulator also questioned the deployment of personnel during blood donation drives after finding that an individual listed as a counsellor was not part of the approved blood bank staff. The hospital described the person as a volunteer engaged in social work, but regulators held that official records must clearly identify authorised personnel performing designated functions. Manpower was among the more serious concerns. Despite collecting more than 5,000 blood units annually, the facility had only two Blood Transfusion Officers and one Medical Social Worker, according to the order. Hospital authorities cited pending recruitment proposals and assistance from resident doctors. Regulators, however, said staffing requirements prescribed under law could not be replaced by temporary arrangements.
Inspectors further documented shortcomings in inventory management and storage monitoring. Temperature records for the quarantine refrigerator were unavailable for verification, while stock registers were not maintained in the prescribed format. The regulator concluded that inadequate documentation affected the traceability and accountability expected in blood banking operations.
Biomedical waste disposal procedures were incomplete, while records of follow-up counselling for sero-positive donors were unavailable during the inspection. After considering the inspection findings, written submissions and oral arguments, FDA Joint Commissioner and Licensing Authority V T Jadhav concluded that regulatory intervention was warranted.
“I have come to the conclusion that the said licensee is not following the provisions of said Act & Rules thereunder,” Jadhav stated in the order. He noted that several explanations furnished by the institution were “not satisfactory” and concluded that suspension was necessary “in the interest of public health at large.” Dr Yogendra Patil, head of the WR-run blood bank, said the FDA’s concerns were limited to documentation and had no impact on blood safety. “The notice concerns documentation requirements. There were no issues with blood safety, testing, drug stocks or patient services,” Patil said. He added that the NABH-accredited blood bank would appeal the notice.

Regulatory Agencies.url_match_title: Endovia Says CannEpil FDA Submission, Meeting Request Coming This Week - The Marijuana Herald
Regulatory Agencies.content:
Endovia Health Sciences says it plans to make its next Food and Drug Administration (FDA) submission for CannEpil in the coming week and request a meeting with the agency to discuss the cannabinoid drug’s regulatory and development pathway.
CannEpil is a pharmaceutical-grade oral formulation made with isolated cannabidiol (CBD) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). The drug was originally developed for drug-resistant epilepsy, and Endovia holds exclusive worldwide rights to develop and commercialize it for human and veterinary uses.
In an announcement issued Monday, Endovia said it intends to request a pre-submission conference with the FDA to discuss how CannEpil could advance through the agency’s regulated drug-development process.
“CannEpil is our first major asset within that strategy, and we expect to make our next FDA submission in the coming week and request a pre-submission conference with the FDA,” said Endovia CEO Brady Cobb.
The company has not announced that CannEpil has received FDA approval, and the planned meeting represents an early regulatory step rather than an authorization to market the drug in the United States.
Endovia acquired the exclusive global rights to CannEpil in July. Its license covers drug-resistant and refractory epilepsy, seizure disorders and related neurological conditions in humans. The company later expanded the agreement to cover veterinary uses.
The veterinary program has already reached a separate FDA milestone. On August 25, the agency’s Center for Veterinary Medicine established an Investigational New Animal Drug file for CannEpil, formally beginning the regulatory process for its development as an investigational veterinary pharmaceutical. Endovia is initially pursuing the drug for cancer-related pain in companion animals, beginning with dogs.
Endovia said Monday that it is also evaluating additional cannabinoid formulations and intellectual property for potential licensing, acquisition or collaboration.
The company tied its broader development strategy to the evolving federal marijuana policy environment, including federal support during recent Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) proceedings for moving marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act. Endovia said its strategy, however, does not depend on federal legalization of adult-use marijuana.

Regulatory Agencies.content:
Food and Drug Administration
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Food and Drug Administration approved Revolution Medicines Inc.’s Rasonque for certain adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after a clinical trial showed the drug nearly doubled median overall survival compared with standard chemotherapy, adding a treatment option for one of the deadliest major cancers.
Rasonque, also known as daraxonrasib, is approved for adults who have received at least one previous systemic therapy or are not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy, the FDA reported. The once-daily tablet inhibits multiple forms of RAS, a protein that drives tumor growth in most patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
In a randomized, open-label trial involving 500 adults with previously treated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, median overall survival reached 13.2 months among patients receiving Rasonque, compared with 6.7 months for those receiving standard chemotherapy.
READ:
FDA Clears Abbott Device to Continuously Track Ketones, Glucose
“This drug showed unprecedented results in an area of high unmet need,” Angelo de Claro, director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence, stated.
The approval came 6.5 months before the agency’s user-fee deadline, according to de Claro, following an expedited regulatory process that included Breakthrough Therapy and Orphan Drug designations and Priority Review.
The application was also reviewed through the FDA Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program, which is designed to accelerate reviews of therapies addressing designated national public-health priorities.
READ:
FDA Clears Abbott Device to Continuously Track Ketones, Glucose
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma accounts for an estimated 90% to 95% of the roughly 67,000 new pancreatic cancer cases diagnosed annually in the U.S., according to National Cancer Institute data cited by the FDA.
Although pancreatic cancer represents about 3.2% of cancer diagnoses, pancreatic adenocarcinoma contributes disproportionately to cancer mortality because it is frequently detected late, progresses aggressively and historically has had limited treatment options.
“Today’s approval provides a critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer,” Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas stated.
READ:
FDA Clears Abbott Device to Continuously Track Ketones, Glucose
The FDA had issued a “safe to proceed” letter in May allowing Revolution Medicines to initiate an expanded-access treatment protocol, providing qualifying patients access to the investigational drug before its approval under applicable federal regulations.
The most commonly reported side effects of Rasonque include rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, decreased appetite and hemorrhage.

Regulatory Agencies.url_match_title: FDA Seizes Cigarette-Shaped Sweets In Accra, Arrests Seller - 3music.tv
Regulatory Agencies.content:
The Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) has seized quantities of an unregistered confectionery shaped like cigarettes in Accra’s Central Business District, with one person arrested over the sale of the product.
The product, branded “Cigarette Rod Lollipop”, was seized during an enforcement operation carried out by the FDA and National Security over the weekend.
The suspect, who is in police custody, is assisting investigations into the importation, distribution and sale of the sweets, the FDA said in a statement issued on Monday, 31 August.
The operation followed public complaints and social media posts about the sale of the cigarette-shaped sweets at Makola Market.
The FDA said the product has not been registered with the Authority, meaning its composition has not been assessed and approved under Ghana’s food safety requirements.
It has advised members of the public not to buy or consume the product.
The Authority also raised concerns about the appearance of the confectionery, particularly its potential effect on children.
It said cigarette-shaped products could help normalise smoking behaviour among children and undermine efforts to prevent tobacco use.
The seizure also relates to Ghana’s restrictions on the depiction and advertising of tobacco products.
Under the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851) and the Tobacco Control Regulations, 2016 (L.I. 2247), the depiction and advertising of tobacco and tobacco-related products are prohibited.
Separately, Section 97(1) of Act 851 makes it an offence to manufacture, import, export, distribute, sell or expose food for sale without the required registration. The FDA said the confectionery falls within the definition of food under the law and is therefore subject to registration requirements.
The FDA has asked traders and individuals who may still have the sweets in stock to contact the Authority or surrender the products at the nearest FDA office.
It has also appealed to members of the public to report anyone selling the sweets or other suspected unregistered food products.
The Authority said information leading to the arrest of importers or others involved in the distribution of the product would be treated confidentially and could attract a reward.
The FDA’s action forms part of its wider market surveillance and enforcement mandate. The regulator says it has zero tolerance for unregistered imported products and can confiscate or dispose of regulated products brought into Ghana without the required approval. (Food And Drugs Authority)
The FDA is responsible for regulating food, drugs, cosmetics, medical devices, household chemicals and tobacco products in Ghana under the Public Health Act. Its enforcement work includes inspections, investigations, product recalls and action against products that do not meet regulatory requirements.

Regulatory Agencies.content:
U.S. financial and health regulators are formalizing closer coordination as disclosures tied to drug approvals and other FDA actions continue to affect listed companies and investors. The new agreement sets a three-year framework for information sharing and joint support on oversight and compliance across the life sciences sector.
Highlights
SEC and FDA signed a three-year Memorandum of Understanding to facilitate coordinated regulatory and enforcement efforts impacting market integrity and public health.
The agreement establishes protocols for interagency information sharing, aiming to improve oversight where FDA developments affect federal securities law obligations and disclosures.
The MOU increases scrutiny on how companies report FDA-related events, enhancing transparency and potentially affecting valuations, trading, and investor confidence in life sciences.
Three-year framework for regulatory coordination
As announced by
SEC
, the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Food and Drug Administration have entered into a Memorandum of Understanding aimed at supporting their respective roles in protecting market integrity and public health.
The agreement establishes a framework for cooperation in regulatory and enforcement work, including protocols for sharing information relevant to both agencies. The arrangement is intended to improve market oversight and compliance where FDA-related developments intersect with federal securities law obligations.
SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins says disclosures related to the FDA by public companies have a significant effect on U.S. markets. He says the FDA is an important partner in administering and enforcing applicable disclosure requirements under federal securities laws, and adds that he expects the MOU to deepen that relationship.
Implications for life sciences transparency
Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantras J.D. says the partnership with the SEC is meant to enhance transparency across the life sciences sector. He says more streamlined information sharing helps protect patients who rely on FDA-regulated products while also supporting public trust in healthcare innovation.
The MOU remains in effect for three years and can be extended or modified with the written consent of both agencies. The arrangement underscores closer scrutiny of how companies communicate FDA-linked developments that can influence valuations, trading activity and investor confidence.
In our earlier article on the Trump administration’s voluntary drug pricing
agreements, we covered plans for a new round of deals aimed at pushing U.S. medicine prices closer to “most favored nation” levels referenced abroad. We noted that participating drugmakers were expected to expand discounts tied to Medicaid, but the ultimate patient savings and real-world impact were still uncertain given existing discount rules.

Regulatory Agencies.content:
Table Of Contents
The Securities and Exchange Commission and the Food and Drug Administration
announced
on August 31, 2026, that they have entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) designed to assist the agencies in carrying out their respective missions of ensuring the integrity of the financial markets and protecting public health.
The MOU establishes a framework for the agencies to enhance cooperation in their regulatory and enforcement responsibilities in order to improve market oversight and compliance. Among other things, it includes information-sharing protocols to facilitate the exchange of information between the SEC and FDA that is relevant to both agencies’ missions.
“FDA-related disclosures by public companies have a significant impact on our markets,” SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins said in the announcement. “The FDA is a valuable partner in our efforts to administer and enforce applicable disclosure requirements under the federal securities laws, and I look forward to further strengthening our partnership through the MOU.”
“We are proud to partner with the SEC to enhance transparency across the life sciences sector,” Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said. “Streamlining our information-sharing helps protect both the patients who rely on FDA-regulated products and the public trust that drives healthcare innovation.”
According to the
text of the agreement
, the agencies intend to facilitate the exchange of information related to FDA-regulated products and activities. The MOU states that the collaboration is expected to bolster informed decision-making, improve the effectiveness of the parties’ oversight and compliance efforts, and ensure that information relevant to public health and the integrity of financial markets is appropriately shared in accordance with applicable laws and policies.
The document describes the FDA’s authority to enforce the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, under which the agency directs its activities toward ensuring the safety, efficacy, and security of drugs, biological products, veterinary products, medical devices, and radiological products, the safety and security of foods and cosmetics, and the regulation of the manufacturing, marketing, and distribution of tobacco products. The SEC’s mission, as described in the MOU, is to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation. The commission oversees broker-dealers, investment companies, investment advisers, clearing agencies, transfer agents, and credit rating agencies, among others, and is responsible for reviewing the disclosures and financial statements of all public companies in the United States. The MOU states that this includes situations where a firm engaged in FDA-regulated activities may have disseminated false or misleading statements to the investing community, such as representations about the status of FDA review, product approvals, clinical trial results, or other matters within the FDA’s regulatory authority that could affect investors’ decisions.
Information-Sharing Protocols
Under the agreement, each party intends to share appropriate information related to FDA-regulated products and activities, and to persons and firms that manufacture, distribute, and sell FDA-regulated products, where practicable. Each party will establish a mechanism, such as a mailbox, for receiving requests for information from the other party, and a mechanism to provide non-public information, such as via secure file transfer. The MOU defines non-public information as information that is not generally available to the public and that is provided, received, or otherwise shared between the parties in connection with the agreement, whether communicated orally, electronically, in writing, or in any other form.
The Food and Drug Division of the HHS Office of the General Counsel, also known as the FDA Office of the Chief Counsel, advises the FDA on legal issues relating to the MOU, serves as the FDA lead for referrals to the SEC of potential violations, and serves as the FDA lead when an SEC matter is in civil or judicial adjudication. Each party will establish and maintain at least one principal point of contact. The FDA will have at least one from its Office of the Chief Counsel, while the SEC will have at least one from its Division of Enforcement and at least one from its Division of Corporation Finance.
The initial contacts named in the MOU are Gabriel Eckstein, associate director of the Division of Corporation Finance’s Disclosure Review Program, and Frank Correll, assistant chief counsel in the Division of Enforcement’s Office of Chief Counsel, for the SEC; and Shannon Singleton, deputy chief counsel for litigation in the FDA’s Office of the Chief Counsel, and Elizabeth Miller, associate commissioner in the FDA’s Office of Inspections and Investigations, for the FDA.
Confidentiality Provisions and Terms
Information sharing under the MOU is governed by existing regulations. When the FDA shares information with the SEC, the exchange is governed by 21 C.F.R. 20.85, under which the SEC may use non-public information received from the FDA to inform any public-company filing review to ensure compliance with the federal securities laws and in connection with any enforcement investigation, proceeding, or civil action within the SEC’s jurisdiction. The SEC cannot provide non-public information received from the FDA to any person who is not an officer, employee, or contractor of the SEC without the FDA’s written permission. The SEC’s sharing of information with the FDA is governed by 17 C.F.R. 240.24c-1, under which non-public information may be provided upon a showing that it is needed and provided the FDA gives assurances of confidentiality that the SEC deems appropriate.
The MOU further states that the FDA will not share trade secret or confidential commercial information whose disclosure is prohibited by specified statutory provisions except as those provisions allow. It sets out procedures for handling Freedom of Information Act requests for shared information, for notifying the providing party of third-party attempts to obtain shared non-public information through compulsory process, and for responding to requests from duly authorized committees of the United States Congress. The parties intend that sharing non-public information under the MOU will not constitute public disclosure or a waiver of confidentiality or any privilege.
The agreement states that it is not for use in sharing public information, requesting testimony, or responding to a subpoena for records or testimony, and that it applies only to requests for information made after its effective date. The document also states that it does not create binding, enforceable obligations against either party, that activities under it are subject to the availability of personnel, resources, and funds, and that it does not affect or supersede any existing or future understandings or arrangements between the agencies.
The MOU became effective upon the signature of both parties, with the signatures of Atkins and Diamantas each dated August 31, 2026, and it will continue in effect for a period of three years. It may be extended, modified, or terminated by the parties’ mutual written consent, and it may be terminated by one party upon 30 days’ advance notice to the other.

There is an old Washington rule worth remembering: Never let a temporary emergency become a permanent business model. That is precisely what is happening with mass drug compounding.
Large-scale compounding was supposed to be an emergency pressure valve. When an FDA-approved medicine became genuinely scarce, compounders could step into the breach and help make sure patients were not left without treatment. It was an accommodation born of necessity, not an invitation to create a shadow pharmaceutical industry. Somewhere along the way, the exception began swallowing the rule.
Today, too much entrepreneurial energy in compounding is chasing GLP-1s, peptides and other commercially attractive products while America continues to struggle with shortages of pediatric cancer medicines, sterile injectables and other lifesaving drugs. The market has discovered something Washington apparently has not: There is considerably more money to be made chasing consumer demand than rescuing an old generic injectable from shortage.
That should make us angry. More importantly, it should make us rethink the bargain.
Compounding has an important place in American medicine. A pharmacist preparing an individualized medicine for a patient who cannot use an FDA-approved formulation is practicing compounding as it was intended. And when a genuine shortage threatens patient care, responsible large-scale compounders can provide an important bridge.
But a bridge is something you cross. You don't build condominiums on it.
The GLP-1 explosion exposed the fundamental weakness in the system. Congress and the FDA created extraordinary flexibility because patients sometimes face extraordinary circumstances. Yet once blockbuster demand emerged for medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, the economic incentives changed dramatically. An emergency authority designed around medical necessity became an enormously attractive commercial opportunity.
FDA has begun pushing back. In April, the agency proposed excluding semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the list of bulk substances that 503B outsourcing facilities may use based on clinical need. FDA's conclusion was straightforward: When approved products are available, it found insufficient evidence of a clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound these drugs from bulk substances.
That is an important distinction. A drug shortage is a public-health problem. A popular drug is a market phenomenon. They are not the same thing, and our regulatory system should stop pretending otherwise. This is regulatory arbitrage, not public health. And now the same entrepreneurial energy is moving aggressively into peptides.
Browse the offerings surrounding today's longevity, weight-loss, anti-aging and wellness businesses and you encounter an expanding alphabet soup of peptides promoted for everything from metabolism and recovery to wound healing and body composition. BPC-157. TB-500. MOTS-C. Ipamorelin. KPV. These are no longer names confined to obscure scientific discussions. They are becoming products, brands and business opportunities.
FDA itself is wrestling with the implications. In July, its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee considered BPC-157, KPV, TB-500 and MOTS-C-related substances for possible inclusion on the list of bulk substances that traditional 503A compounders may use. That discussion is evidence of something much larger than an argument over a handful of molecules. Compounded peptides are becoming a regulatory category in their own right.
That should set off alarm bells.
Peptides aren't innocuous simply because they sound cutting-edge, biological or "personalized." Manufacturing and characterizing peptide products can present complicated questions involving impurities, aggregation and immunogenicity. FDA has specifically raised such concerns about several peptides being used or proposed for compounding. For some, the agency says it lacks basic human exposure or safety information.
Think about what that means. If a pharmaceutical company wanted to market a new peptide as a drug, we would expect it to characterize the molecule, demonstrate manufacturing consistency, investigate toxicology, conduct clinical trials and ultimately provide FDA with evidence sufficient to demonstrate safety and effectiveness. We would debate endpoints, statistical power, adverse events, benefit-risk and manufacturing quality.
But attach the word "compounded" to an increasingly commercialized peptide marketplace and suddenly some people behave as though those questions become optional. They don't. We should be encouraging peptide science. We should be accelerating responsible peptide drug development. Some of these molecules may ultimately prove enormously valuable. But scientific promise is an argument for generating evidence, not an excuse for avoiding it.
There is an important difference between personalized medicine and personalized pharmacology-by-marketing. We are in danger of blurring it. The distinction matters because FDA approval still means something. An FDA-approved medicine has been reviewed for safety, effectiveness, manufacturing quality, labeling and consistency. A compounded preparation does not become equivalent to an FDA-approved drug simply because it contains an ingredient with the same or similar name. It enters the marketplace through a fundamentally different regulatory pathway with different safeguards.
Patients deserve to understand that difference. They also deserve a system in which pharmaceutical capacity responds to public-health need rather than internet demand.
Consider the obscenity of the juxtaposition. America can summon remarkable entrepreneurial energy to sell popular weight-loss formulations and trendy peptides, yet physicians can still find themselves worrying about access to old, inexpensive medicines used to treat children with cancer and other critically ill patients.
We have somehow constructed a pharmaceutical marketplace in which the economic signal can be strongest precisely where the medical emergency is weakest. That isn't resilience. It is market failure wearing a lab coat. Congress should revisit the rules with a simple principle in mind: Emergency compounding privileges should serve emergency medical needs.
When an FDA-approved medicine is genuinely unavailable, compounding should remain an option. When an individual patient has a legitimate clinical need that cannot be met by an approved product, traditional pharmacy compounding should remain available. Those are important functions worth protecting. But the definition of shortage cannot become a commercial loophole, and the end of a shortage must mean something.
Under current FDA policy, 503B outsourcing facilities generally cannot make essentially copies of approved drugs. The shortage exception is just that—an exception. FDA permits greater flexibility when an approved drug appears on its shortage list, but once that shortage ends, the justification for mass production of copies begins disappearing with it.
That principle should be enforced rather than endlessly negotiated. And we should go further.
If Washington believes large-scale compounding is an important component of national pharmaceutical resilience—and I believe it can be—then policymakers should create incentives that reward compounders for doing the difficult, economically unattractive work the nation needs. Pediatric oncology drugs. Sterile injectables. Critical-care medicines. Essential generic products with fragile supply chains. Medicines for which a manufacturing interruption can become a clinical crisis overnight. Those are the products that justify extraordinary regulatory flexibility.
Rather than allowing compounding policy to be driven predominantly by where consumer margins are fattest, Congress and FDA should ask how compounding capacity can be incorporated deliberately into America's drug-shortage strategy. That could include stronger incentives for production of designated critical medicines, better federal visibility into what outsourcing facilities are producing, and faster mechanisms for directing qualified capacity toward emerging shortages.
The objective should not be to punish legitimate compounders. It should be to reconnect privilege with purpose. It also means stronger enforcement against businesses effectively operating as unapproved pharmaceutical manufacturers while sheltering themselves beneath rules designed for pharmacy compounding. It means refusing to allow temporary shortages of enormously popular branded medicines to become the foundation for permanent copycat industries. And it means establishing a much clearer regulatory boundary around the rapidly expanding peptide business before commercial practice outruns regulatory policy.
There is another uncomfortable question policymakers should ask: What happens to investment in the next generation of medicines if successful innovation automatically creates an alternative commercial market operating under substantially different rules?
Drug development is expensive, risky and frequently unsuccessful. The FDA approval standard is intentionally demanding. Companies spend years generating evidence, validating manufacturing processes and demonstrating that the medicine in the vial or injector is reliably the medicine described on the label.
Those requirements aren't bureaucratic decorations. They are the foundation of pharmaceutical credibility.
If the reward for surviving that gauntlet is an indefinitely expanding marketplace of compounded substitutes—or an adjacent marketplace in which experimental molecules can be commercially popularized without first traveling the same evidentiary road—Washington should not be surprised when the economics of innovation begin to change.
None of this requires eliminating compounding. It requires remembering why we permit it.
America needs a pharmaceutical system capable of responding rapidly when conventional manufacturing fails. Drug shortages are real. They hurt patients, exhaust clinicians and expose dangerous weaknesses in our supply chains. Compounding can and should be part of the solution.
But only if we stop confusing the existence of demand with the existence of an emergency.
A child waiting for a cancer medicine is an emergency. A hospital unable to obtain a critical injectable is an emergency. A patient requiring a customized formulation unavailable from an FDA-approved manufacturer presents a legitimate medical need. A booming commercial market for fashionable weight-loss drugs, anti-aging injections and experimental peptides is something else entirely. That isn't a drug shortage. It is a new pharmaceutical marketplace trying to borrow the regulatory privileges created for an emergency.
The pharmaceutical supply chain will always follow incentives. If policymakers want compounding capacity directed toward medicines that save lives during shortages, they need to make that the attractive proposition rather than merely hoping corporate altruism will overpower economics. The original compact was sensible: When the conventional drug supply fails patients, compounding can temporarily fill the gap. Let's restore that compact. Compounding should be a fire department, not a franchise opportunity.
Peter J. Pitts, a former FDA Associate Commissioner, is President of the Center for Medicine in the Public Interest.

Traditional & Complementary Medicine.content:
New partnership to promote herbal, traditional medicine
Society
August 31, 2026 - 14:9
TEHRAN – A memorandum of understanding has been signed between the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology and Knowledge-Based Economy and the Inter-Islamic Network on Nanotechnology (INN), aimed at expanding scientific and technological cooperation, fostering networking among research centers and knowledge-based companies, and strengthening the international presence of Iran’s traditional medicine capabilities and its herbal and natural products.
The agreement also aims to expand scientific and technological cooperation, foster networking between research centers and knowledge-based companies, and enhance the international presence of the country’s traditional medicine, herbal and natural products, IRNA reported.
Technological development and the conversion of scientific achievements into effective economic and technological capacities require the establishment of transboundary collaboration networks and connections among universities, research centers, specialists, knowledge-based companies, and scientific and technological institutions to pave the way for knowledge sharing, the implementation of joint projects, and the development of international markets.
One of the main objectives of the MOU is to establish a network of influential international agents, identify and benefit from the capacities of knowledge-based companies and experts, for example, the Standing Committee for Scientific and Technological Cooperation (COMSTECH), facilitate interactions among research and scientific centers, and provide a platform for the implementation of joint research projects and initiatives.
According to the MOU, INN will help boost ties between domestic and international scientific and technological networks, which can contribute to recognizing scientific partners in Islamic countries, and enhancing collaborations between knowledge-based companies and research centers.
The adopted approach will enhance scientific and technological diplomacy, expedite the development of joint research, knowledge and experience exchange, and technology transfer, improve product standards, promote technological collaborations, and ultimately expand regional and international markets for Iranian knowledge-based products in medicinal plants and Persian medicine.
According to a report by the World Health Organization (WHO), Iran ranks third in traditional medicine trials in the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), highlighting the country’s status as one of the world’s pioneers in traditional and complementary medicine.
China and India rank first and second, respectively, the health ministry’s website reported.
The share of clinical trials in traditional and complementary medicine in Iran makes up about three percent of all clinical trials registered in the country, while just about 0.3 percent of the healthcare staff are experts in traditional and complementary medicine. The report shows the high capacity of Iranian researchers to move towards evidence-based medicine.
Persian traditional medicine strongly focuses on prioritizing health maintenance and disease prevention over treatment.
It is one of the most ancient forms of traditional medicine. It is grounded in the concept of four senses of humor: phlegm (Balgham), blood (Dam), yellow bile (Safra’), and black bile (Sauda’). The concept of the four senses of humor is based on the teachings of Rhazes and Avicenna in an elaborate medical system.
So far, about 30,000 plant species have been identified in the world, with Iran’s share of about 8,000 species, which is more than the whole of the species found in Europe.
Around 500 Persian medicine experts are providing health and medical treatment services across the country. More than 1,000 general practitioners who have passed the Persian medicine courses approved by the health ministry are also offering services.
Training Persian medicine experts has always been at the top of the Persian medicine office’s agenda. Therefore, different skill courses have been developed and held under the supervision of the health ministry.

Traditional & Complementary Medicine.url_match_title: Experts Seek Clinical Data, Quality Standards to Boost Global Acceptance of Traditional Medicine - Radio Nigeria Lagos
Traditional & Complementary Medicine.content:
GENERAL NEWS
HEALTH
LAGOS
For plant-based remedies to gain global acceptance, they must be backed by solid clinical data and strict quality standards.
That was the key takeaway from experts during a virtual forum hosted by the Nigeria Natural Medicine Development Agency on mark this year’s African Traditional Medicine Day.
Consultant Endocrinologist Professor Andrew Oloko from Bayero University led the call for action, urging significant investment in clinical research, stronger regulatory bodies, and upgraded quality control labs.
He stressed that these foundations are critical for integrating traditional medicine into the continent’s healthcare system.
Speaking from Geneva, the World Health Organization’s Head of the Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine Unit , Dr. Kim Sungchol echoed that sentiment.
He pointed to the vast potential of traditional medicine and suggested that this year’s event could help shape government policie, from licensing to quality control, to build a more structured and effective ecosystem.
Adding to the discussion, public health advocate Chief Temitayo Erogbogbo emphasized the need to document the knowledge of older generations, creating formal structures within communities to preserve these breakthroughs.
The Director General of the NNMDA, Professor Martin Emeje, stressed that biomedicine and traditional medicine are not in competition, arguing that traditional remedies are uniquely positioned to achieve Universal Health Coverage by being accessible, affordable, and high-quality.
The DG announced that the agency has begun a national digital documentation drive to catalogue traditional medicines.
The consensus among participants, including practitioners from across Nigeria and medicinal farmers from Kenya, was that the future of Africa’s health lies in honouring the knowledge of the past, not by developing in isolation, but through collaboration and formal recognition.
They all agreed that the WHO’s Global Traditional Medicine strategy provides the roadmap to ensure that universal access to healthcare is not just a goal, but a reality.
Written by Olusegun Haastrup

Traditional & Complementary Medicine.content:
Dr Njoroge Kimani, biochemist and toxicologist, showcasing juice made from wheatgrass. (Photo: Charity Kilei)
Wheatgrass, the young green shoot of the common wheat plant, is attracting growing interest as a source of nutrients and natural compounds that may support human health.
For more than a decade, Dr Njoroge Kimani, a clinical biochemist and toxicologist, has been studying the plant to understand its safety, nutritional value, and potential role in supporting people living with chronic illnesses.
Unlike the wheat commonly used to make bread, flour, and other foods, wheatgrass is harvested while the plant is still young and green, before it develops into mature wheat grain. It can be consumed as fresh juice, dried into powder, added to food, or taken in capsule form.

For Dr Njoroge, the interest in wheatgrass is not simply about following a health trend. It is the result of years of research and experimentation aimed at understanding what the plant contains and how it interacts with the body.
“I have been working on this to determine its efficacy and safety because safety is key,” Dr Njoroge said.
His work with wheatgrass dates back more than a decade. He says he began investigating the plant around 2014, including clinical and laboratory research designed to examine its potential effects and safety.

The scientist says one of the things that initially attracted him to wheatgrass was its nutritional composition. According to him, the plant contains vitamins, minerals, amino acids, dietary fibre, and plant-based protein.
“Wheatgrass is one of the richest products with vitamins, amino acids, minerals, dietary fibre and protein,” he said.
He argues that obtaining all these nutrients from individual foods can sometimes require eating a variety of fruits and vegetables, while wheatgrass can provide several of them in a concentrated form.
But wheatgrass, he explains, is more than just a source of nutrients.
Wheatgrass in its seedling stage. (Photo: Charity Kilei)
The plant also contains what scientists refer to as bioactive compounds, substances that may have biological effects in the body even though they are not considered essential nutrients in the same way as vitamins and minerals.
Dr Njoroge says his interest has particularly focused on compounds associated with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, as well as compounds that may influence immune responses.
Inflammation, he explains, is not always visible.
“When people talk about inflammation, they think about trauma or something that you can see swelling,” he said. “But there are inflammations that occur inside the body.”
He says some of the compounds found in wheatgrass may help regulate such processes. He also points to compounds that have been investigated for their possible antimicrobial, antioxidant, and other biological effects.
For Dr Njoroge, one of the most interesting areas of wheatgrass research is its potential relevance to chronic illnesses such as diabetes and hypertension, conditions that require long-term management and are increasingly affecting populations in Kenya and around the world.
He says he has used wheatgrass products among patients with different health conditions, including diabetes and hypertension, while studying how the plant may support overall health.
The scientist explains that chronic illnesses are often influenced by several processes in the body, including inflammation, oxidative stress, and changes in metabolism. This is where he believes the nutrients and bioactive compounds found in wheatgrass could potentially play a role.
He points to antioxidant compounds that may help protect cells from oxidative stress and compounds that may influence inflammatory processes. His research has also examined the plant’s possible effects on blood glucose.
However, Dr Njoroge’s claims about managing chronic illnesses should be viewed alongside the current level of scientific evidence. While laboratory and animal studies may show promising biological effects, they do not automatically mean that wheatgrass can treat or prevent diabetes, hypertension, cancer, or other chronic diseases in humans.
For people already taking medication, wheatgrass should therefore not be viewed as a replacement for prescribed treatment.
His research has included laboratory studies using rats as animal models. Dr Njoroge says wheatgrass extracts were administered through different routes, including orally and intraperitoneally.
Researchers subsequently examined blood samples and different organs to determine how the extracts affected the animals.
“We checked various organs,” he said, explaining that different enzymes and other biological markers were analysed.
The work was designed to answer one of the most important questions surrounding any health product: Is it safe?
Variety of wheatgrass products including capsules, powder, and juices. (Photo: Charity Kilei)
Dr Njoroge says his findings encouraged him to continue investigating wheatgrass, including its potential effects on blood glucose and its safety in animal models.
Some of his research was published in the
International Journal of Medicine and Pharmaceutical Sciences
in 2020. He said the publication included research on the in vivo potential safety and glycaemic effects of aqueous extracts of wheatgrass.
Research involving animals, however, is only one stage of the scientific process. More robust human clinical research is necessary to establish whether the benefits observed in laboratory and animal studies translate into meaningful health benefits for people.
One of the things Dr Njoroge finds appealing about wheatgrass is its accessibility.
“You can grow it within your backyard,” he said. “We can adapt it and grow it anywhere.”
He says Kenya has a favourable environment for growing the plant, although wheatgrass can also be cultivated indoors under controlled conditions.
The product is available in several forms, including fresh juice, dried powder, freeze-dried powder, and capsules.
The powder can be mixed with water or incorporated into food, while capsules provide a convenient option for people who do not want to prepare or drink wheatgrass juice.
Dr Njoroge says wheatgrass is not intended only for people living with particular illnesses. He views it as a product that can also contribute to general nutrition and health maintenance.
“Everybody, whatever their health status, can use it for maintenance of good health,” he said.
Despite his years of research, Dr Njoroge says locally developed herbal and complementary health products still face difficulties reaching the wider market.
One of the biggest challenges, he says, is government support.
He welcomes the increasing attention being given to traditional and complementary medicine within the Ministry of Health, saying health-related products need proper scientific evaluation, regulation, and oversight.
“Anything health is with the Ministry of Health,” he said.
Public perception is another challenge.
Dr Njoroge believes Kenyans can sometimes have greater confidence in medicines and health products developed outside the country while overlooking research and innovations produced locally.
He also says multinational companies have an advantage when it comes to marketing and public visibility.
For him, the answer is not to reject conventional medicine but to allow locally developed products to undergo rigorous scientific investigation and, where evidence supports their use, receive appropriate recognition.
Dr Njoroge Kimani explaining the health benefits of wheatgrass. (Photo: Charity Kilei)
Wheatgrass is only one part of Dr Njoroge’s scientific journey.
He points to his previous research on environmental health, including work on lead in petrol and the health effects associated with the Dandora waste dumping site.
He says he was also recognised for his research work at Kenyatta National Hospital, where he received an award for being the best researcher in 2010.
His work, he says, has consistently been driven by an interest in understanding how environmental and biological factors affect people’s health.
Today, that interest has brought him back to a plant that can be grown in an ordinary backyard.
But as wheatgrass becomes increasingly popular, Dr Njoroge acknowledges that enthusiasm must be matched by evidence.
The plant contains nutrients and bioactive compounds that make it scientifically interesting, and early research has identified potential biological effects. But claims that wheatgrass can prevent or treat serious illnesses require stronger evidence from well-designed human studies.
For Dr Njoroge and other scientists working in traditional and complementary medicine, the planned integration could mark a significant step forward, particularly by opening up greater opportunities for research funding and public access to scientific findings.
Dr Njoroge says increased investment would help researchers conduct further studies, document indigenous knowledge, and make credible research on traditional remedies more accessible to the public. He believes Kenyans should be able to access reliable information about locally developed treatments and understand what has been scientifically established about their safety and effectiveness.
Research into traditional and complementary medicine is already being carried out in different institutions, including the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) and other research laboratories. Scientists are studying various medicinal plants and therapies in an effort to understand their potential benefits, safety, and possible applications in healthcare.
For researchers, the goal is to bridge the gap between Kenya’s rich traditional knowledge and modern scientific evidence, ensuring that promising discoveries do not remain confined to laboratories but can, where proven safe and effective, eventually benefit the wider public.
Dr Njoroge Kimani explaining the health benefits of wheatgrass. (Photo: Charity Kilei)
What appears to be ordinary grass, he says, could become part of a much bigger conversation about nutrition, chronic illness, and Kenya’s ability to turn its natural resources into safe, scientifically evaluated health products.
Speaking during African Traditional Medicine Day, Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale called for an evidence-based approach to integrating traditional medicine into Kenya’s healthcare system, saying indigenous medical practices must be scientifically researched, validated, and properly regulated before they can be incorporated into mainstream healthcare.
Duale said the government is at an advanced stage of finalising a policy framework that will guide the evaluation, regulation, and promotion of traditional medicine while ensuring that its use is safe, effective, and supported by credible scientific evidence.
The government plans to integrate traditional medicine into Kenya’s healthcare system by 2028, with the policy framework expected to provide a pathway for assessing and regulating traditional remedies before they are incorporated into formal healthcare services.
He emphasised that African traditional medicine should complement modern healthcare rather than operate as a parallel system, noting that the two approaches can work together where there is sufficient evidence of safety and effectiveness.
“Our duty is to preserve what is valuable while ensuring that every intervention offered within the healthcare system is safe, effective and supported by evidence,” Duale said.
He noted that traditional medicine is deeply rooted in Africa’s biodiversity, culture, and indigenous knowledge, and remains widely used because it is accessible, affordable, and culturally acceptable to many communities.
However, Duale stressed that cultural value and widespread use alone should not justify integrating traditional remedies into the formal healthcare system.
He said traditional practices and products must undergo proper research, documentation, scientific validation, and quality testing to establish their safety, effectiveness, appropriate use, and potential risks.
The planned integration by 2028 is expected to strengthen recognition of traditional medicine while protecting patients from unsafe or ineffective products and practices.
It could also create opportunities for researchers to identify traditional remedies with genuine therapeutic potential and subject them to the same scientific scrutiny required of other health interventions.

Greenheal Net is a health and wellness website focused on natural remedies, self-care, and healthier lifestyle choices. For people who prefer simple wellness information rather than highly technical explanations, the website brings different health-related topics together in one place.
A review of the current Greenheal website shows three main areas on its homepage: Natural Remedies, Self-Care, and

. The site describes itself as a family-owned platform created by parents with the goal of supporting holistic well-being.
However, natural does not automatically mean safe, and online wellness information should not replace professional medical care. This guide explains what greenheal net currently offers, how readers can use its information responsibly, and what to check before following health advice found online.
What Is Greenheal Net?
Greenheal net refers to Greenheal.net, a health and wellness content website that describes itself as a “hub for holistic wellness.”
The current homepage highlights three primary areas:
Natural Remedies
Self-Care
Healthy Lifestyle
The website says its mission is to help people explore holistic well-being through practical information and resources. Its “Our Story” page also describes Green Heal as a family-owned platform created by parents.
This positioning makes the website primarily useful as an informational resource.
Visitors may encounter articles about herbs, supplements, wellness routines, nutrition, fitness, emotional well-being, skincare, recovery, healthy habits, and other lifestyle subjects.

What Is the Purpose of Greenheal Net?
The main purpose of greenheal net appears to be making wellness information easier for everyday readers to explore.
Many health topics become difficult to understand when they contain complicated medical terms. Greenheal generally uses a consumer-oriented article format and divides its content into recognizable categories.
Its stated philosophy places emphasis on holistic well-being.
Holistic wellness generally means considering different parts of a person’s lifestyle rather than concentrating on one issue alone. For example, a healthy routine may involve nutrition, sleep, physical activity, emotional health, stress management, and preventive care.
The site’s current homepage describes its Healthy Lifestyle category as offering information for cultivating a more balanced life, while its Self-Care section focuses on practices intended to support personal well-being.
1. Natural Remedies on Greenheal Net
Natural remedies are one of the most visible parts of greenheal net.
Greenheal describes this section as covering traditional remedies, herbal solutions, and
holistic wellness
approaches. Its recent content includes discussions involving supplements and common natural remedies.
Natural wellness topics may include:
Herbs
Vitamins
Supplements
Nutrition
Home remedies
Sleep
Hydration
Stress management
Lifestyle changes
These topics attract people who want to understand options beyond conventional everyday wellness routines.
However, this is also an area where readers need to be especially careful.
Natural Does Not Mean Risk-Free
A plant-based product can still have biological effects on the body.
Herbs and dietary supplements may interact with prescription medicines or may not be appropriate for certain people. The appropriate amount can also depend on factors such as age, health status, medication use, pregnancy, and other individual circumstances.
Before trying a remedy found on greenheal net or another wellness website, ask:
Is there reliable evidence supporting the claim?
Are possible side effects explained?
Could it interact with medication?
Is dosage discussed responsibly?
Does the author have relevant expertise?
Are credible medical or scientific sources provided?
Does the article explain who should avoid the remedy?
For significant health decisions, discuss the information with a qualified healthcare professional.
2. Self-Care Content
Self-care is another major topic on greenheal net.
The website has a dedicated Self-Care category containing articles about physical and emotional well-being, recovery, healthy aging, habits, and other lifestyle issues.
Self-care does not need to mean buying expensive wellness products.
Simple practices may include:
Maintaining a regular sleep schedule
Taking breaks from long periods of sitting
Spending time outdoors
Exercising regularly
Eating balanced meals
Maintaining supportive relationships
Managing everyday stress
Making time for hobbies
Setting realistic personal boundaries
A useful self-care routine should also be realistic.
Trying to completely change your diet, exercise routine, sleep schedule, and daily habits at the same time can be difficult to maintain.
Gradual improvements are often easier to continue.
3. Healthy Lifestyle Information
Greenheal net healthy lifestyle information featuring nutrition mindful eating and everyday wellness habits
The third major content area on greenheal net is healthy living.
The website describes its Healthy Lifestyle category as offering tips and advice intended to support a balanced lifestyle.
Healthy living is a broad subject.
It can include nutrition, physical activity, sleep, stress management, home environment, personal routines, and preventive health habits.
A basic healthy lifestyle may involve:
1. Eating a balanced diet:
Focus on a variety of
nutritious foods
rather than following extreme diets without professional guidance.
2. Getting regular movement:
Walking, cycling, swimming, sports, strength training, and other appropriate activities can all contribute to an active lifestyle.
3. Getting enough sleep:
Consistent sleep habits support everyday physical and mental functioning.
4. Managing stress:
Relaxation, exercise, social connection, hobbies, and mindfulness practices may help people deal with everyday stress.
5. Getting appropriate medical care:
Lifestyle habits complement healthcare; they do not replace necessary examinations, screenings, vaccinations, diagnoses, or treatments.
Who Is Greenheal Net For?
Greenheal net may appeal to readers who want straightforward introductions to health and wellness topics.
That could include:
Adults exploring healthier habits
People interested in natural wellness
Readers researching self-care
Families looking for general wellness information
People interested in herbs and supplements
Readers exploring nutrition and lifestyle topics
People interested in holistic living
However, the type of information you need matters.
Someone researching ideas for building a healthier daily routine has very different needs from someone experiencing chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, a serious allergic reaction, or another medical emergency.
Online wellness content is not an appropriate substitute for emergency or professional medical care.
Is Greenheal Net a Medical Website?
Readers should understand an important distinction.
Greenheal net is best treated as a general wellness information resource rather than a substitute for individualized medical care.
A website article cannot examine you physically, review your complete medical history, perform laboratory tests, check your current medications, or make a reliable diagnosis based on your personal circumstances.
This distinction becomes especially important when content discusses:
Diseases
Symptoms
Mental health
Pregnancy
Supplements
Prescription medicines
Chronic pain
Serious injuries
Medical treatments
You can use an online article to learn terminology or prepare questions for a medical appointment.
You should not assume that reading an article means you have diagnosed yourself correctly.
How to Check Health Information on Greenheal Net
Because greenheal net operates in the health and wellness space, readers should develop a simple fact-checking process.
Check the Author
Start by identifying who wrote the article.
Greenheal currently displays author names on its articles, and its homepage also highlights content attributed to health and wellness coach Vejki Luiket.
But a name alone does not establish expertise.
Ask whether the writer’s qualifications match the subject being discussed.
For example, experience in fitness does not automatically make someone qualified to give advice about prescription drugs.
Check the Sources
Good health content should make important claims verifiable.
Look for references to recognized sources such as:
Government health agencies
Medical organizations
Universities
Peer-reviewed research
Hospitals
Qualified professional associations
A source is particularly important when an article makes a specific claim about treating, preventing, or diagnosing a condition.
Check the Publication Date
Medical knowledge changes.
Advice that was considered reasonable several years ago may have been updated as new research became available.
Look for publication or update dates, particularly when researching medications, supplements, treatments, medical procedures, or safety recommendations.
Compare Important Claims
Never depend on one website for an important medical decision.
If an article makes a significant health claim, compare it with information from reliable healthcare organizations.
Agreement across high-quality independent sources gives you a stronger basis for understanding the topic.
Greenheal Net and Herbal Remedies
Greenheal net herbal remedies guide exploring natural ingredients traditional wellness practices and holistic health approaches
Herbal remedies are popular because plants have been used in traditional practices for generations.
But “traditional” and “scientifically proven” are not identical concepts.
Some plant compounds have been studied extensively. Others have limited or mixed evidence for particular uses.
Greenheal itself publishes content discussing herbs and natural remedies, including topics such as turmeric, ginger, ashwagandha, honey, and peppermint.
When researching an herb, consider four questions.
What is it supposed to do?
Identify the exact claim rather than assuming the herb is good for “overall health.”
What evidence supports that use?
Look for high-quality human research when possible.
What are the risks?
Consider side effects, allergies, interactions, and contraindications.
Who should avoid it?
Pregnancy, certain medical conditions, age, and medication use can change the risk profile.
Greenheal Net and Sustainable Wellness
Another theme appearing in Greenheal’s content is environmentally conscious or sustainable living.
Its story page connects the platform’s wellness mission with sustainable living, while newer articles discuss eco-health practices and environmentally conscious lifestyle choices.
Sustainable wellness can involve small choices rather than dramatic lifestyle changes.
Examples might include reducing unnecessary waste, preparing more meals at home, choosing reusable products when practical, improving household ventilation, and making thoughtful purchasing decisions.
However, readers should avoid assuming that a product is healthier simply because it is marketed as “green,” “clean,” “natural,” or “eco-friendly.”
Marketing language is not the same as scientific evidence.
Greenheal Net and Online Health Safety
Health websites deserve extra scrutiny because incorrect advice can have real consequences.
One particularly useful observation from researching greenheal net is that some pages on the site make claims about Greenheal itself that do not appear consistently across the current public website.
For example, individual Greenheal articles have described features such as health tracking, wellness reports, programs, trackers, and other tools, while the current homepage primarily presents Greenheal as a content platform organized around wellness articles.
That inconsistency is a reason to verify a feature directly before assuming it exists.
Readers should distinguish between:
What the website demonstrably provides and what an individual article says the website provides.
This principle applies to every website, not just Greenheal.
Privacy and Personal Information
Privacy is another factor to consider when using any health-related website.
Before subscribing to newsletters, creating accounts, completing forms, or providing personal information, read the website’s current privacy policy.
Pay attention to:
What information is collected
Why it is collected
Whether cookies are used
Whether data is shared
How long information is retained
How users can contact the website
Whether users can request changes or deletion where applicable
Avoid sharing unnecessary medical or personal information through ordinary website forms.

Greenheal net is a wellness-focused website built around natural remedies, self-care, and healthy lifestyle information. Its creators describe it as a family-owned platform inspired by their experience as parents seeking holistic approaches to family well-being.
The website can provide a starting point for people interested in learning more about wellness habits, herbs, supplements, sustainable living, and self-care. However, readers should remember that health information requires a higher standard of scrutiny than ordinary lifestyle content.

Selon les médias du régime, l’inflation officielle en août de cette année, par rapport à août de l’an dernier, s’élevait à 89 %, tandis que l’inflation des produits alimentaires et des boissons atteignait 127 %, dépassant même les 150 % dans certaines provinces (Centre de statistiques d’Iran, 28 août). Bien entendu, le taux d’inflation réel est encore plus élevé. Parallèlement, la crise liée à la pénurie de médicaments et à la flambée des prix a pris des proportions bien plus importantes, rendant la vie nettement plus difficile pour les travailleurs, les ouvriers et les salariés.
Hadi Ahmadi, porte-parole de l’Association iranienne des pharmaciens, a déclaré à ce sujet : « Le prix des médicaments a augmenté en moyenne d’environ 80 % depuis le début de l’année, et pour certains produits, cette hausse a atteint 300 % » (Eghtesad Online, 28 août 2026). En d’autres termes, l’inflation annuelle des médicaments s’élève en moyenne à environ 200 %, pouvant aller pour certains jusqu’à 700 %.
L’un des principaux facteurs limitant l’accès aux médicaments est la dette colossale du régime envers les pharmacies. En détournant depuis de nombreuses années les cotisations d’assurance maladie prélevées sur les salaires des employés et des travailleurs, le régime n’a pas remboursé aux pharmacies le coût des médicaments. Selon Ettelaat Online, « la dette de 20 000 milliards de tomans des compagnies d’assurance envers les pharmacies a conduit nombre d’entre elles au bord de la faillite » (28 août 2026).
La crise du secteur pharmaceutique en Iran est un problème de longue date qui s’aggrave de jour en jour. La cause profonde de ce problème réside dans le fait que, depuis des années, la production et la distribution des médicaments sont monopolisées par le siège du Guide suprême Khamenei. Cette question revêt une importance encore plus cruciale étant donné que, selon le Dr Hojjatollah Yazdanshenass, ancien président de l’Association iranienne des pharmaciens, « 97 % des médicaments dont le pays a besoin sont produits localement » (Quotidien Azerbaïdjan, 16 septembre 2020).
Ces monopoles sont concentrés au sein de deux grandes institutions, le Groupe pharmaceutique Barekat et la Société d’investissement pharmaceutique Tamin (TPICO), toutes deux contrôlées par le siège de Khamenei. Le Groupe pharmaceutique Barekat a été créé en 2010 et gère plus de 15 filiales, dont Alborz Darou, qui contrôle elle-même 11 filiales (site de la société Barekat).
Tamin Pharmaceutical (TPICO) compte au total 26 filiales actives dans la production, la distribution et d’autres secteurs. L’une des filiales majeures de TPICO est la société Darou Pakhsh, qui emploie 4400 personnes (site SHASTA).
Pour illustrer l’ampleur du pillage perpétré par ce monopole pharmaceutique ces dernières années, prenons deux exemples. Le quotidien officiel Shargh écrivait en 2022 : « Un médicament produit localement pour un coût de 500 000 tomans, et dont la chaîne de distribution est totalement transparente, est vendu 25 millions de tomans » (28 février 2022). Cela signifie que le prix de vente au détail du médicament est gonflé jusqu’à atteindre 50 fois son coût de production.
Dans un autre cas, Pirsalehi, ancien directeur de l’Agence nationale des aliments et des médicaments, a déclaré : « Certaines injections qui coûtaient auparavant 5000 ou 6000 tomans atteignent désormais 19.000 tomans » (journal Arman-e Emrouz, 3 mars 2025).
Tant que le régime inhumain des mollahs restera au pouvoir, la pauvreté, l’inflation et la corruption continueront de s’aggraver. La seule solution réside dans un soulèvement visant à renverser ce régime et à instaurer la démocratie et la souveraineté populaire.

participer à cette démarche baptisée
« longue vie aux
médicaments »
.
Au total, environ
73 spécialités
pharmaceutiques
ont été identifiées comme candidates
potentielles pour bénéficier d’une extension de leur date de
péremption. Une réponse massive qui témoigne de la volonté du
secteur de réduire le gaspillage.
De trois à cinq ans de conservation pour certains
antidouleurs
Parmi les médicaments concernés figurent des traitements
largement utilisés par les Français. Le paracétamol, la
lévothyroxine, la mélatonine ou encore le lithium sont dans la
liste.
Découvrez aussi :
Forte chaleur : ces médicaments très courants peuvent
devenir dangereux
Les célèbres
Efferalgan et Dafalgan
, fabriqués
par le laboratoire UPSA, pourraient voir leur durée de vie passer
de 36 à 60 mois. Un gain de deux années complètes qui pourrait
transformer la gestion des stocks.
Améliorer la disponibilité sans toucher aux formules
Cette initiative ne prévoit aucune modification de la
composition des médicaments. Il s’agit uniquement d’une
réévaluation scientifique
de leur stabilité dans
le temps.
Les industriels devront réaliser une batterie de tests
rigoureux. Ces analyses visent à démontrer que les propriétés
thérapeutiques restent intactes sur la période de conservation
étendue.
Un double objectif sanitaire et économique
L’ANSM vise à résoudre deux problématiques majeures
simultanément. D’une part,
réduire le gaspillage
considérable généré par les médicaments jetés prématurément.
D’autre part, améliorer la disponibilité des traitements
essentiels. Les ruptures de stock, devenues fréquentes ces
dernières années, pourraient être atténuées grâce à cette
mesure.
Découvrez aussi :
Éclipse du 12 août : les risques pour les yeux et
comment les éviter
Des modifications réglementaires nécessaires
Pour concrétiser ces extensions, les laboratoires devront
déposer des demandes officielles. Ces requêtes concernent la
modification de l’autorisation de mise sur le
marché
, un processus strictement encadré.
L’agence sanitaire examine actuellement les dossiers soumis. Les
premiers changements sur les boîtes de médicaments pourraient
intervenir dans les prochains mois, sous réserve de validation
scientifique.
